title: Common Source Bias – when everyone repeats the same thing
description:
You watch the news, read blogs, study research – and everywhere you see the same thing? It seems like solid information, but if all sources refer to the same origin, it’s just an echo, not verification.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- News – different headlines, but all reporting the same study.
- Reviews – bloggers praise a new gadget, but they all rely on the same press release.
- Research – dozens of studies confirm a hypothesis, but they all use the same dataset.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Check the original source – where did the information come from?
- Compare methodologies – are the studies truly independent?
- Think critically – if everyone is saying the same thing, it doesn’t always mean it's true.

title: Conservatism Bias – when new evidence doesn't change old beliefs
description:
You receive new information, but it barely changes your opinion? That’s Conservatism Bias – the tendency to insufficiently revise one's beliefs even when presented with new evidence.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Finance – you hold onto a stock despite news that the company is struggling.
- Science – new research disproves old theories, but you find it hard to accept the change.
- Personal life – someone has changed, but you still judge them by their past actions.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Double-check facts – new isn’t always better, but ignoring updates is risky.
- Question old beliefs – the world evolves, maybe your views should too.
- Stay flexible – adapting to new data makes you smarter and better at decision-making.

title: Functional Fixedness – when objects can only be used one way
description:
Do you see an object and think it can only be used for its intended purpose? That’s Functional Fixedness – the tendency to perceive an object only in its traditional role, ignoring other possible uses.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Everyday life – scissors are just for paper, even though they can open packages.
- Work – a familiar tool doesn’t solve a new task, but you don’t look for alternatives.
- Problem-solving – solutions are searched for in obvious places, even when a creative approach might work better.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Think broader – every object can have multiple uses.
- Experiment – try unconventional approaches.
- Train creativity – the more variations you see, the fewer mental limits you have.

title: Clustering Illusion – when randomness looks like a pattern
description:
Do you see patterns where none exist? That’s Clustering Illusion – the tendency to overestimate the importance of small streaks, clusters, or runs in large sets of random data.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Gambling – three black numbers in roulette? You think red is ‘due’ next (it’s not).
- Stock market – believing you can ‘read’ chart patterns to predict movements.
- Sports – assuming a player is ‘on fire’ because of a lucky streak, even when it's just statistics.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Understand randomness – streaks and patterns happen even without real meaning.
- Don’t rely on intuition in statistics – our brain sees patterns even when they don’t exist.
- Look at large datasets – isolated cases don’t prove a trend.

title: Illusory Correlation – when you see a connection that isn’t there
description:
Do you think two events are connected when it’s just coincidence? That’s Illusory Correlation – the tendency to see a relationship between unrelated things.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Stereotypes – “People with tattoos commit more crimes,” even though statistics don’t support it.
- Medicine – “I took a vitamin and my cold went away,” but it might have healed naturally.
- Finance – “The stock market drops when the moon is in a certain phase,” but correlation doesn’t mean causation.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Check the data – correlation ≠ causation.
- Consider context – two things happening together doesn’t mean one causes the other.
- Be skeptical of gut instincts – many ‘obvious’ connections fall apart under real analysis.

title: Pareidolia – when your brain sees patterns that aren’t there
description:
Do you see faces in clouds or hear ‘hidden messages’ in music? That’s pareidolia – the tendency to perceive random images or sounds as meaningful.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Clouds – they seem to form shapes like animals or faces.
- The Moon – you see a face on it, but it’s just a pattern of craters.
- Music – some people hear words in random noises or reversed recordings.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Understand that your brain seeks familiar patterns – it’s an evolutionary feature, not reality.
- Be skeptical – if you see something unusual, ask yourself: is it real or just an illusion?
- Test your perception – try looking at the same image from different angles, and the illusion may disappear.

title: Anthropocentric Thinking – when everything is judged by human standards
description:
Do you assume animals think and feel just like humans? That’s Anthropocentric Thinking – the tendency to use human experiences as the basis for understanding everything else, even if it operates on completely different principles.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Animals – “A dog is smiling, so it must be happy” (but bared teeth might signal stress).
- Nature – “Trees take care of their children,” though it’s just biological processes.
- The Universe – “The universe wants something from us,” but that’s just human projection.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Remember that the world doesn’t revolve around humans – other creatures and systems have their own rules.
- Learn scientific explanations – emotions and behaviors in nature often differ from human ones.
- Be open to changing perspectives – if something seems ‘human-like,’ it might not actually be.

title: Anthropomorphism – when objects and animals get human traits
description:
Do you think your cat feels offended or that a robot has emotions? That’s Anthropomorphism – the tendency to attribute human traits, emotions, or intentions to animals, objects, or abstract concepts.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Pets – “My cat is angry because I didn’t feed him” (he’s just reacting to hunger).
- Technology – “My car is in a bad mood today” (no, it’s just a mechanical issue).
- Nature – “The Moon looks sad” – but it has no emotions, that’s just our perception.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Separate reality from perception – objects and animals don’t think like humans.
- Look for scientific explanations – animal behavior is often driven by instincts, not emotions.
- Be mindful – humans naturally see human traits everywhere, but that doesn’t mean they exist.

title: Attentional Bias – when your thoughts control what you see
description:
Do you notice only what’s on your mind? That’s Attentional Bias – the tendency to focus on information related to your current thoughts or concerns while ignoring everything else.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Shopping – you want a new car and suddenly see it everywhere.
- Fears – afraid of plane crashes, so you feel like they happen all the time.
- Relationships – convinced people dislike you, so you only notice signs of rejection.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Understand that perception isn’t always objective – your brain adjusts reality to fit your thoughts.
- Practice mindfulness – be aware of what you focus on.
- Question your conclusions – are you seeing the full picture or just a selective part?

title: Frequency Illusion – when something new suddenly appears everywhere
description:
Did you recently learn about something and now it seems to be everywhere? That’s Frequency Illusion (also known as the Baader-Meinhof Phenomenon) – a cognitive bias that makes us think something appears more frequently than before, when in reality we’ve just started noticing it.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Shopping – you learn about a new phone model, and suddenly everyone seems to have it.
- Names – you meet someone with a rare name, and now you hear it everywhere.
- Trends – you hear a new term, and suddenly it’s being used all around you (even though it was always there).

💡 How to avoid it?
- Recognize that your brain is playing tricks on you – things aren’t appearing more often, you’re just noticing them more.
- Focus on data, not feelings – if something seems more frequent, check the actual numbers.
- Be skeptical of your memory – just because something caught your attention doesn’t mean it became more common.

title: Implicit Association – when your brain links things faster than you realize
description:
Do some words or concepts seem to connect faster in your mind than others? That’s Implicit Association – the effect where the speed of linking words depends on how closely they seem related, even if the connection is subjective.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Stereotypes – you associate ‘man’ with ‘engineer’ faster than ‘woman’ with ‘engineer,’ even if you don’t believe in gender differences.
- Advertising – a brand feels successful because it’s always shown in that context.
- Decision-making – something seems right simply because your brain links it more quickly.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Slow down and analyze – fast associations don’t always mean truth.
- Develop critical thinking – question why you link some things faster than others.
- Be aware of cultural influence – many connections come from external factors, not personal experience.

title: Salience Bias – when the striking overshadows the relevant
description:
Do you focus only on the most striking things while ignoring the less noticeable ones? That’s Salience Bias – the tendency to concentrate on the most prominent details, even when they are not the most important.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- News – scary headlines grab attention, even if the actual risk is low.
- Finance – investors react to recent dramatic events instead of long-term trends.
- Decision-making – choices are based on what stands out, not what makes the most sense.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Evaluate data, not emotions – just because something is striking doesn’t mean it’s important.
- Look for the full picture – the unnoticed details might be more relevant than the loud ones.
- Be wary of media and advertising – they exploit salience to manipulate your attention.

title: Selection Bias – when the sample doesn’t reflect reality
description:
Are you making conclusions based on a sample that doesn’t represent the whole picture? That’s Selection Bias – an error that occurs when data is not randomly selected and doesn’t reflect reality.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Surveys – asking only social media users excludes offline opinions.
- Medicine – testing a drug on young volunteers doesn’t reveal its effects on older patients.
- Business – successful startups seem common because failures are rarely reported.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Check who’s in the sample – is it truly representative?
- Look for missing groups – who was excluded from the data?
- Be cautious with generalizations – if information comes from a limited group, it may distort reality.

title: Survivorship Bias – when you only see the winners
description:
Do you think success is just a matter of making the right choices because all you see are winners? That’s Survivorship Bias – the tendency to focus on those who ‘made it’ while ignoring those who didn’t because they’re invisible.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Business – startups seem like an easy path to riches because no one talks about the thousands that failed.
- Self-improvement – you read success tips from millionaires but don’t see those who followed the same advice and got nowhere.
- History – planes return with bullet holes, and engineers reinforce those areas, forgetting about the ones that never made it back.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Ask: who are we not seeing? – if you only look at success stories, you’re missing half the picture.
- Find complete data – survivors aren’t the only ones who went through the process.
- Remember, successes are more visible than failures – but that doesn’t mean they’re more common.

title: Quantification Bias – when only measurable things seem to matter
description:
Do you trust numbers more than anything else? That’s Quantification Bias – the tendency to give more weight to measurable data while ignoring what can’t be easily quantified.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Work – a manager evaluates performance only through KPIs, ignoring team morale.
- Education – universities focus on test scores but overlook creativity and motivation.
- Medicine – relying only on lab results while ignoring how the patient actually feels.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Remember that not everything important can be measured – emotions, motivation, and intuition also matter.
- Find a balance – numbers are useful, but without context, they can mislead you.
- Don’t let metrics dictate decisions – sometimes qualitative factors outweigh quantitative ones.

title: Well-Travelled Road Effect – when familiar routes feel faster
description:
Does your daily commute feel shorter than a new route of the same distance? That’s Well-Travelled Road Effect – the tendency to underestimate travel time on familiar routes and overestimate it on unfamiliar ones.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Trips – the way home feels shorter than the way there, even though it's the same distance.
- Work – new tasks seem longer and harder than routine ones, even if they take the same time.
- Travel – getting to a new place feels exhausting, but the return trip feels faster.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Remember that time perception is subjective – familiar routes require less mental effort.
- Focus on facts, not feelings – the travel time is the same both ways.
- Don’t avoid new routes – the unfamiliar only feels longer at first.

title: Normalcy Bias – when you believe nothing bad will happen
description:
Do you believe disasters only happen to others, not you? That’s Normalcy Bias – the tendency to ignore or underestimate the likelihood of rare but serious events just because they haven’t happened before.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Natural disasters – people refuse to evacuate before a hurricane because “nothing bad has happened before.”
- Financial crises – investors don’t believe in a market crash until it actually happens.
- Health – “I’ve never been sick, so I’ll be fine,” even when symptoms clearly indicate a problem.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Accept reality, not comfortable beliefs – just because something hasn’t happened doesn’t mean it won’t.
- Assess risks in advance – it’s better to prepare than to assume you’ll be lucky.
- Learn from others’ mistakes – disasters have happened before, and you’re not immune.

title: Effort Justification – when hard work makes something seem more valuable
description:
Does something feel more valuable just because you worked hard for it? That’s Effort Justification – the tendency to overvalue things that required significant effort, even if the outcome isn’t objectively worth it.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Furniture assembly – the IKEA effect: if you built a cabinet yourself, it seems better than a pre-assembled one.
- Relationships – after years in a difficult relationship, it’s hard to admit it was a mistake.
- Career choices – spending years in a job you hate makes it hard to accept a different path might’ve been better.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Separate effort from actual value – hard work doesn’t always make something better.
- Be honest with yourself – don’t hold onto things just because you invested in them.
- Focus on the future – what matters is not what you spent, but whether it benefits you now.

title: Ben Franklin Effect – when doing a favor makes you like someone more
description:
Do you like someone more after doing them a favor? That’s Ben Franklin Effect – when we’ve already helped someone, we’re more likely to help them again, convincing ourselves that we like them.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Colleagues – you help a coworker once, and suddenly feel more positively toward them.
- Relationships – you do a favor for someone you were neutral about, and now they seem more likable.
- Manipulation – some people exploit this effect by asking for small favors to build your trust.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Notice how your attitude changes – do you genuinely like the person, or are you just justifying your actions?
- Be wary of manipulation – if someone frequently asks for small favors, it may be intentional.
- Use it to your advantage – if you want someone to warm up to you, ask them for a small favor first.

title: Backfire Effect – when evidence makes false beliefs stronger
description:
Do you double down on your beliefs when confronted with contradicting evidence? That’s Backfire Effect – the tendency to not just reject inconvenient facts, but to become even more convinced of your original belief.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Politics – you show someone undeniable proof that their candidate is lying, but they support them even more.
- Science – anti-vaxxers see scientific evidence but instead of reconsidering, their belief in a conspiracy deepens.
- Personal life – you prove to a friend that their partner is cheating, and they start defending them even harder.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Be open to changing your mind – resisting facts is a sign of cognitive dissonance.
- Avoid aggressive persuasion – softer arguments work better than direct confrontation.
- Notice when facts annoy you – sometimes, the information that frustrates you the most is exactly what you need to hear.

title: Congruence Bias – when you only test what you want to confirm
description:
Do you test a hypothesis only in ways that confirm it, rather than trying to disprove it? That’s Congruence Bias – the tendency to seek evidence that supports an idea while ignoring alternative explanations.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Science – a researcher runs tests that confirm their theory but doesn’t check for other possible causes.
- Business – a company tests if an ad campaign works but doesn’t analyze what else might be driving sales.
- Personal life – convinced a friend is upset with you, you look for signs but don’t consider other explanations for their behavior.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Look for counterexamples – test not just confirming but also disproving evidence.
- Be open to alternatives – your explanation may not be the only one.
- Ask questions, don’t make assumptions – a good test challenges rather than just confirms.

title: Experimenter’s Bias – when you see only what you expect
description:
Do you only notice results that confirm your hypothesis? That’s Experimenter’s Bias – the tendency to give more weight to data that aligns with expectations while downplaying or ignoring conflicting results.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Science – a researcher ‘accidentally’ focuses only on data that supports their theory while dismissing the rest as error.
- Medicine – a doctor believes a new drug works, so they notice only improvements while ignoring failures.
- Workplace – a manager assumes certain employees are more capable and notices only their successes while overlooking others’ potential.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Question your expectations – do you want your hypothesis to be right, or do you want the truth?
- Accept all data, not just the convenient ones – inconvenient results may be more valuable than expected ones.
- Trust the numbers, not intuition – our perception adapts to expectations, but statistics remain objective.

title: Observer-Expectancy Effect – when wanting a result makes it appear
description:
Does a researcher believe in a certain outcome and unconsciously shape the data to fit? That’s Observer-Expectancy Effect – when an experimenter unintentionally influences results by modifying the experiment or interpreting data in a biased way.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Science – a researcher expecting a drug to work notices improvements even where none exist.
- Education – a teacher expects better performance from ‘gifted’ students and grades them more leniently.
- Sports – a referee unconsciously calls more fouls against a team they view negatively.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Use blind methods – don’t know the expected results beforehand to avoid influencing them.
- Record data objectively – avoid interpreting results to fit expectations.
- Ask yourself: what if I expected the opposite? – this helps view the data without bias.

title: Selective Perception – when you only see what you expect
description:
Do you notice only what confirms your expectations while ignoring everything else? That’s Selective Perception – the tendency to filter information through existing beliefs and disregard anything that doesn’t fit.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Politics – supporters of different parties watch the same news but interpret it completely differently.
- Sports – fans believe the referee is biased against their team, even when mistakes happen on both sides.
- Personal life – someone convinced they’re unappreciated only sees signs of being ignored but overlooks praise.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Recognize that perception is subjective – what you see isn’t always the full reality.
- Consider alternative perspectives – try viewing the situation through someone else’s eyes.
- Be open to unexpected facts – if the data contradicts your expectations, maybe it’s not the data that’s wrong, but your filter.

title: False Consensus Effect – when you think everyone agrees with you
description:
Do you believe most people share your opinions and choices? That’s False Consensus Effect – the tendency to overestimate how much others agree with you.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Politics – you assume ‘all reasonable people’ support your views because your social circle does.
- Work – you think your idea is obviously the best, and you're shocked when colleagues disagree.
- Social media – you believe your opinions are widespread because your feed only shows similar views.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Remember that your circle isn’t the whole world – people with different views exist, even if you don’t interact with them.
- Check actual statistics – not all social media trends reflect the majority’s opinion.
- Be open to other perspectives – if a belief feels ‘obvious,’ ask yourself: am I just surrounded by like-minded people?

title: False Uniqueness Bias – when you think you’re more unique than you are
description:
Do you believe your ideas, talents, or projects are one of a kind, while others are just average? That’s False Uniqueness Bias – the tendency to overestimate how special you are and underestimate how many others share similar qualities.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Work – you’re convinced no one else can handle tasks as well as you do.
- Creativity – you think your idea is groundbreaking, only to discover someone has already done something similar.
- Social skills – you assume your values and perspectives are rare, even though many people share them.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Check how truly unique your idea is – it might already exist in another form.
- Acknowledge that others are competent too – being good doesn’t mean others are bad.
- Use others’ achievements as inspiration, not a threat – uniqueness often comes from refining existing ideas.

title: Forer (Barnum) Effect – when vague statements feel deeply personal
description:
Have you ever read a horoscope or personality test and thought, “This is so me!”? That’s Forer (Barnum) Effect – the tendency to believe vague descriptions are uniquely accurate for you, even though they apply to most people.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Astrology – “You are intelligent but sometimes doubt yourself.” Sounds right? But it applies to nearly everyone.
- Fortune telling – predictions feel personal, but they’re worded vaguely enough to fit many people.
- Personality tests – you take a quiz, and the results ‘nail’ your traits, yet thousands of others get the same result.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Look for specifics – if a statement is broad and could fit anyone, it probably does.
- Remember that your brain seeks confirmation – if you want to believe it, you’ll find reasons to.
- Be skeptical of pop psychology – real personality analysis is deeper than flattering generalizations.

title: Illusion of Asymmetric Insight – when you think you understand others better than they understand you
description:
Do you think you see through people, but they don’t understand you? That’s Illusion of Asymmetric Insight – the tendency to overestimate how well you know others while believing they don’t understand you as well.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Relationships – you believe you understand people’s motives, but assume your own actions remain a mystery to them.
- Work – you think you’ve figured out your colleagues’ personalities but underestimate how well they see your weaknesses.
- Social media – you assume you can ‘decode’ people based on their posts but ignore how you also curate your own image.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Remember, you’re not a mind reader – people are more complex than they seem.
- Acknowledge that others observe you too – you’re not the only ‘deep’ thinker.
- Don’t judge based on first impressions – if you think you’ve figured someone out instantly, chances are you haven’t.

title: Illusion of Control – when you think you have more influence than you do
description:
Do you believe your actions influence events that are actually out of your control? That’s Illusion of Control – the tendency to overestimate your ability to manage external circumstances.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Gambling – you throw dice in a ‘special’ way, believing it affects the outcome.
- Work – you assume a project's success is entirely in your hands, ignoring external factors.
- Personal life – you believe you can change someone’s behavior if you try hard enough.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Separate what you can control from what you can’t – focus your efforts where they actually make a difference.
- Don’t mistake randomness for causation – sometimes, things just happen regardless of your input.
- Evaluate outcomes objectively – if you truly have control, your influence should be consistent and predictable.

title: Illusion of Transparency – when you think people can read your mind
description:
Do you think others understand your thoughts and emotions as clearly as you do? That’s Illusion of Transparency – the tendency to overestimate how much others perceive your mental state and how well you understand theirs.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Conversations – you assume your nervousness is obvious, but others don’t even notice.
- Work – you expect your boss to know you want a raise, even though you’ve never said anything.
- Relationships – you believe your partner ‘should just know’ how you feel without you explaining.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Don’t expect people to read your mind – if something matters, say it clearly.
- Remember that emotions aren’t as visible as you think – your feelings are less obvious to others than they are to you.
- Clarify what others think – don’t rely on assumptions, ask directly.

title: Illusion of Validity – when you think your judgments are more accurate than they are
description:
Do you believe your judgments are accurate just because the available information fits together well? That’s Illusion of Validity – the tendency to overestimate the accuracy of one’s judgments, especially when data appears logically consistent.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Finance – an investor assumes their market predictions are correct because past guesses were right.
- Career – an HR manager believes they can perfectly identify top candidates, ignoring past hiring mistakes.
- Logic – if multiple facts form a coherent story, it feels true, even if it’s just a coincidence.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Don’t confuse coherence with accuracy – even the most logical scenarios can be wrong.
- Look for validation beyond your own logic – check the data, not just your intuition.
- Allow room for error – if you feel 100% certain, chances are you’re overlooking something.

title: Illusory Superiority – when you think you’re better than most people
description:
Do you think you drive better than the average driver? Or that your decisions are more rational than most people’s? That’s Illusory Superiority – the tendency to overestimate your good qualities and underestimate your flaws compared to others.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Driving – most people believe they are above-average drivers (which is statistically impossible).
- Work – you think you’re more productive than your colleagues, even when no one else notices the difference.
- Intelligence – you assume you’re more logical or insightful than others while ignoring their strengths.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Compare yourself to real data, not just feelings – your self-assessment might be far from objective.
- Acknowledge that everyone has blind spots – if you think you don’t, that’s already a bias.
- Assess yourself honestly – ask others about your weaknesses and be open to hearing the truth.

title: Naïve Cynicism – when you think others are more selfish than you
description:
Do you believe that people act selfishly while your own actions are purely rational and fair? That’s Naïve Cynicism – the tendency to assume others are biased and self-serving, while seeing yourself as objective and sincere.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Work – you assume colleagues are looking out for themselves, but your decisions are purely for the greater good.
- Politics – you believe political opponents manipulate, while your beliefs are based on facts.
- Personal life – you think others make friends for personal gain, but your relationships are entirely genuine.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Acknowledge that everyone has biases – including you – believing you’re purely objective is already a bias.
- Don’t assume hidden motives everywhere – sometimes, people genuinely mean well.
- Be honest with yourself – you may also make choices influenced by self-interest.

title: Naïve Realism – when you think you see the world as it really is
description:
Do you believe your views are based on objective facts, while those who disagree are simply misinformed or biased? That’s Naïve Realism – the tendency to think you see reality as it truly is, while others are clouded by ignorance or irrationality.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Politics – if someone holds different beliefs, you assume they just ‘don’t get it.’
- Online debates – you believe your viewpoint is obvious to any rational person.
- Workplace – you think your colleagues misunderstand a situation simply because they don’t see it the way you do.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Recognize that your reality isn’t the only one – others have different experiences and perspectives.
- Don’t assume disagreement = ignorance – your opponent may have valid points you haven’t considered.
- Practice cognitive humility – even your strongest beliefs might not be as solid as they seem.

title: Overconfidence Effect – when you're sure, but still wrong
description:
Do you say you’re 99% sure about something, only to find out you were wrong? That’s Overconfidence Effect – the tendency to overestimate the accuracy of your knowledge and decisions, even when mistakes are likely.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Quizzes and tests – you mark ‘absolutely sure,’ but mistakes happen more often than you think.
- Business – investors believe they ‘know’ the market, but their predictions fail more than expected.
- Everyday decisions – you’re confident about a memory, yet the details turn out to be incorrect.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Double-check yourself – if you feel completely certain, pause and review the facts.
- Accept the possibility of being wrong – even experts make mistakes, and so can you.
- Be cautious with predictions – confidence doesn’t equal accuracy, especially in complex matters.

title: Planning Fallacy – when you think things will take less time than they do
description:
Did you promise to finish on time, but missed the deadline again? That’s Planning Fallacy – the tendency to underestimate how long a task will take, even when you’ve made the same mistake before.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Work – a project that ‘should take two weeks’ ends up lasting months.
- Studying – you think you’ll prepare for an exam in two days, then find yourself cramming at 3 AM.
- Home renovations – you plan to finish by the weekend, but a month later, it’s still a mess.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Look at past experiences – if it took longer last time, why would this be different?
- Add a time buffer – multiply your optimistic estimate by at least 1.5.
- Expect the unexpected – delays and unforeseen issues always happen.

title: Restraint Bias – when you think you have more self-control than you do
description:
Do you think you can resist temptation, but end up giving in anyway? That’s Restraint Bias – the tendency to overestimate your ability to maintain self-control.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Diets – “I’ll buy chocolate, but I’ll eat it in small pieces,” yet an hour later, the whole bar is gone.
- Finances – you swear you won’t overspend, but suddenly your shopping cart is full of unnecessary items.
- Social media – you just want to ‘check notifications,’ but an hour later, you’re deep into TikTok.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Don’t test your willpower – remove temptations – set up barriers instead of relying on self-restraint.
- Plan ahead – if you know you’re weak in certain situations, create a strategy to avoid them.
- Acknowledge that self-control is limited – it’s easier to avoid temptation than to fight it.

title: Third-Person Effect – when you think media influences others, but not you
description:
Do you believe that advertising, propaganda, or news influence others, but not you? That’s Third-Person Effect – the tendency to think mass media shapes other people’s opinions while leaving your own perception untouched.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Advertising – you think ads manipulate ‘ordinary people,’ but you still choose brands you’ve seen more often.
- News – you assume propaganda affects the masses, but your views are also shaped by the media you consume.
- Social media – you’re sure algorithms mislead others, yet don’t realize how they reinforce your own biases.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Acknowledge that you’re also influenced – no one is completely immune to media effects.
- Be mindful of your choices – why do you prefer one brand over another? Is it really your decision?
- Check your sources and filters – algorithms and media influence everyone, including you.

title: Base Rate Fallacy – when you ignore general statistics for a specific case
description:
Do you trust vivid examples more than dry statistics? That’s Base Rate Fallacy – when general probabilities are ignored in favor of specific cases, even when statistics provide a more accurate prediction.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Medicine – a test for a rare disease comes back positive, and you panic, forgetting that false positives are more common than the disease itself.
- Business – you hear about a startup that became a billion-dollar company and assume you have the same odds, ignoring failure rates.
- Crime – you think forensic evidence is conclusive, without considering how often similar evidence appears among innocent people.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Look at overall numbers, not just stories – rare cases stand out, but they don’t represent the real probability.
- Consider the full probability – even if a test is ‘90% accurate,’ what matters is how common the condition actually is.
- Be wary of success stories – one inspiring exception doesn’t erase thousands of unseen failures.

title: Compassion Fade – when one victim moves you more than a thousand
description:
Do you feel more moved by the story of one child in need than by statistics about millions suffering? That’s Compassion Fade – the tendency to emotionally react to personal stories while ignoring large-scale suffering.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Charity – a single photo of a sick child generates more donations than statistics about millions in need.
- News – a tragic story about one person feels heartbreaking, but large-scale disasters seem distant.
- Politics – one case of injustice sparks outrage, while systemic issues go unnoticed.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Remember that numbers represent real people – statistics hide real lives behind the figures.
- Be aware of emotional bias – just because you only empathize with visible suffering doesn’t mean the unseen is less important.
- Balance emotion with reason – helping individuals matters, but decisions should account for the bigger picture.

title: Conjunction Fallacy – when a specific scenario seems more likely than a general one
description:
Do detailed stories seem more likely than simple ones? That’s Conjunction Fallacy – the tendency to assume that a specific combination of conditions is more probable than a single condition, even though that’s statistically impossible.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- News – “A journalist advocating for women’s rights won the election” seems more likely than just “A journalist won the election.”
- Predictions – “There will be an economic crisis next year due to political instability” feels more plausible than just “There will be an economic crisis next year.”
- Stereotypes – if someone studies philosophy, you assume “A philosopher who loves yoga” is more probable than just “A philosopher.”

💡 How to avoid it?
- Remember that specifics are always less probable than general events – the more conditions you add, the less likely the scenario.
- Don’t fall for compelling narratives – the more detailed a scenario, the more likely it’s just a well-crafted story rather than reality.
- Check your logic – if a detailed event seems more probable than a simple one, stop and think again.

title: Duration Neglect – when the ending matters more than the experience
description:
Does a long enjoyable experience feel no better than a short one if it ended badly? That’s Duration Neglect – the tendency to judge experiences based on their final moments rather than their overall length.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Vacations – a week at a resort with an unpleasant last day feels worse than a short but perfect weekend.
- Pain – a long medical procedure that eased at the end is remembered as less painful than a short but sharp one.
- Movies & books – a bad ending can ruin the memory of an otherwise great story.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Evaluate the whole experience, not just the end – one bad moment doesn’t erase all the good ones.
- Remember that memory is subjective – we recall peak moments, but they don’t define the entire experience.
- Practice mindfulness – enjoy the journey, not just the outcome.

title: Hyperbolic Discounting – when the present matters more than the future
description:
Do you promise to start exercising next week, only to push it back when the time comes? That’s Hyperbolic Discounting – the tendency to prefer immediate rewards over long-term benefits, even if your future self will regret it.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Food choices – when ordering for the week, you pick healthy options, but when choosing for today, you grab chocolate.
- Finances – you spend money immediately instead of saving, even though you know saving is smarter.
- Habits – you delay exercise or studying because present comfort feels more important than future rewards.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Make decisions in advance – if you know you’ll act impulsively, set things up beforehand (e.g., automate savings).
- Create barriers to impulsive choices – for example, don’t keep junk food at home if you want to eat healthy.
- Remember that the future comes faster than you think – your “tomorrow self” won’t be happy with what “today you” decided.

title: Insensitivity to Sample Size – when small samples mislead you
description:
Do you make conclusions based on just a few examples, assuming they reflect reality? That’s Insensitivity to Sample Size – the tendency to underestimate how much small samples can distort results.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Surveys – someone claims to know ‘public opinion’ based on just 10 random responses.
- Business – an entrepreneur tries an ad once, gets a bad response, and decides it doesn’t work.
- Medicine – you hear that two people recovered using an unusual treatment and assume it’s effective.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Check the sample size – the smaller the dataset, the higher the chance of randomness.
- Don’t trust anecdotal evidence – one success story doesn’t prove a trend.
- Look for statistical validation – if something truly works, it should work in large samples.

title: Less-Is-Better Effect – when less seems more valuable
description:
Do you prefer a small but high-quality reward over a larger but less impressive one? That’s Less-Is-Better Effect – the tendency to see a smaller set as more valuable when judged separately, but to prefer the larger set when compared directly.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Gifts – a single luxury pen in a box seems better than a set of five regular pens.
- Business – a customer prefers a restaurant with a refined small menu over one with a broad but average selection.
- Legal judgments – a thief who stole $100 seems worse than one who stole $500 but was fined $50, because the fine softens the perceived damage.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Compare options directly – when evaluated side by side, preferences become more rational.
- Assess actual value, not just presentation – a well-packaged option isn’t always the better one.
- Remember that perception shifts with context – separate evaluations can be misleading.

title: Scope Neglect – when 2,000 and 20,000 victims feel the same
description:
Would you pay the same amount to help 2,000 people as you would for 20,000? That’s Scope Neglect – the tendency to respond emotionally rather than rationally, failing to account for the actual size of a problem.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Charity – people donate the same amount to save 2,000 children as they would to save 20,000.
- Environment – news of 1,000 polluted rivers feels as concerning as 10 polluted rivers, even though the scale is vastly different.
- Disasters – a tragedy with 500 victims evokes the same reaction as one with 5,000, because our brains don’t scale emotions effectively.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Focus on numbers, not just emotions – larger problems should be taken more seriously.
- Assess the impact of actions – is your response proportional to the scale of the issue?
- Be mindful in decision-making – if something sounds tragic, evaluate how truly large it is.

title: Zero-Risk Bias – when eliminating a small risk feels better than reducing a big one
description:
Do you prefer eliminating a small risk entirely rather than significantly reducing a bigger one? That’s Zero-Risk Bias – the tendency to feel safer when a risk is reduced to zero, even if it’s not the most rational choice.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Finance – you pay off a $500 debt completely instead of reducing your main $5,000 debt, even though it would save more on interest.
- Health – you choose a ‘zero-fat’ product, even though it has the same calories as the regular version.
- Environment – millions are spent eliminating 100% of pollution in one river, while the same funds could significantly reduce pollution in multiple rivers.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Compare the impact of decisions – eliminating small risks isn’t always better than reducing bigger ones.
- Don’t chase ‘zero’ at any cost – sometimes reducing a greater threat yields a better result.
- Focus on overall safety – if a choice feels instinctively right, double-check the numbers.

title: Agent Detection Bias – when you see intention behind randomness
description:
Do you feel like strange events happen for a reason, as if someone is behind them? That’s Agent Detection Bias – the tendency to see intent and intelligence behind random events, even when there’s no real agent involved.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Religion & mysticism – unexpected events feel like signs from fate or divine intervention.
- Conspiracy theories – if something goes wrong, it seems like part of a master plan rather than a simple mistake.
- Technology – when your phone freezes or software crashes, you assume it was ‘designed that way’ rather than just a glitch.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Remember that coincidences happen – not every strange event has a hidden meaning.
- Look for simple explanations – if something can be explained by randomness or error, it probably should be.
- Be skeptical of theories requiring complex conspiracies – the world is often chaotic rather than controlled by unseen forces.

title: Automation Bias – when you blindly trust automated systems
description:
Do you follow your GPS even when it leads you into a dead end? That’s Automation Bias – the tendency to over-rely on technology, even when it’s wrong.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Medicine – a doctor follows a flawed diagnostic system without double-checking the results.
- Aviation – a pilot trusts autopilot too much and ignores critical warning signs.
- Everyday life – people blindly follow GPS directions, even when the road is blocked.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Don’t lose critical thinking – automated systems are helpful, but they’re not flawless.
- Trust, but verify – if something seems off, double-check it manually.
- Remember that algorithms make mistakes too – automation is useful, but it doesn’t replace common sense.

title: Gender Bias – when gender shapes expectations
description:
Do you assume engineers are mostly men and teachers are mostly women? That’s Gender Bias – implicit assumptions that lead us to perceive people differently based on gender, even when there’s no rational basis for it.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Careers – assuming women are worse at math or that men can’t be good preschool teachers.
- Language – defaulting to ‘he’ when referring to a person or an animal without gender cues.
- Ability evaluation – expecting men to be better leaders or technical experts while underestimating women in the same fields.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Recognize bias in yourself – if you automatically link jobs to gender, pause and reconsider.
- Judge based on facts, not stereotypes – gender doesn’t determine intelligence, skills, or personality.
- Be mindful of language – if you default to male pronouns in neutral cases, try rethinking that habit.

title: Sexual Perception Bias – when you misread romantic signals
description:
Do you think someone is flirting when they’re just being polite? Or do you miss obvious signals of interest? That’s Sexual Perception Bias – the tendency to either overestimate or underestimate someone’s romantic interest in you.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Overperception Bias – you assume a smile or friendly gesture is flirting when it’s just politeness.
- Underperception Bias – you fail to notice clear signals of interest because you don’t expect them.
- Social norms – men tend to overperceive interest, while women tend to underperceive, leading to miscommunication.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Remember that friendliness ≠ flirting – not every smile has hidden meaning.
- Pay attention to body language – some signals are subtle but real.
- Ask directly if unsure – instead of guessing, clarify with words.

title: Stereotyping – when you judge a person based on their group
description:
Do you think programmers are introverted and athletes aren’t smart? That’s Stereotyping – the tendency to expect people to have certain traits just because they belong to a group, even when you have no actual information about them.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Workplace – assuming young employees are lazy and older ones can’t handle technology.
- Culture – believing all French people are romantic or all Germans are strict, even though individuals vary.
- Gender – expecting men to be better at math and women to be better at caregiving, despite personal differences.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Focus on the person, not the label – people are always more complex than their category.
- Seek evidence for or against your assumptions – evaluate individuals based on real qualities.
- Remember that stereotypes shape your decisions – they can blind you to reality and limit your thinking.

title: Conservatism Bias – when new evidence doesn’t change old beliefs
description:
Do you stick to your beliefs even when new facts contradict them? That’s Conservatism Bias – the tendency to underweight new information and fail to update beliefs sufficiently.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Finance – investors ignore new market trends because they’re attached to old strategies.
- Science – people continue believing outdated theories despite new research.
- Personal life – if you’ve always seen someone as unreliable, even their good actions don’t change your opinion.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Be open to changing your views – if the data says one thing and you believe another, reconsider your stance.
- Separate emotions from facts – old information feels familiar, but it isn’t always correct.
- Seek refutations, not just confirmations – evaluate new evidence as seriously as the old.

title: Functional Fixedness – when objects can do more than you think
description:
Do you hold a screwdriver and not realize you can use it to open a bottle? That’s Functional Fixedness – the tendency to see objects only in their usual roles, even when they have other possible uses.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Daily life – you search for a bottle opener when a spoon or key would work just as well.
- Work – you assume a tool is only for one task when it could be adapted for others.
- Creativity – you miss new solutions because you think only within traditional uses.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Look for unconventional uses – if you’re stuck, think about repurposing what’s around you.
- Train creative thinking – challenge yourself to use familiar objects in new ways.
- Focus on function, not labels – a tool isn’t just what it was designed for.

title: Law of the Instrument – when one tool feels like the answer to everything
description:
When you have a hammer, does everything look like a nail? That’s Law of the Instrument – the tendency to over-rely on familiar tools or methods while ignoring better alternatives.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Work – you apply the same approach to every problem, even when it’s ineffective.
- Management – you rely on strict deadlines for everything, forgetting that flexibility can be key.
- Technology – you always use your favorite software, even when a different tool would work better.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Focus on the problem, not just your usual method – not everything can be fixed with one tool.
- Learn new approaches – maybe you just haven’t explored more effective solutions yet.
- Be adaptable – if something isn’t working, you need a different tool, not more force with the same one.

title: Decoy Effect – when a third option pushes you toward the second
description:
Do you choose between two options, but then a third one appears, making the second option look better? That’s Decoy Effect – a marketing trick designed to push you toward a specific choice.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Shopping – you’re deciding between a $800 phone and a $1,200 premium model. Suddenly, a $1,150 version appears with almost the same specs as the $1,200 one, making the premium model seem like the best deal.
- Restaurants – small coffee for $3, large for $7. Then they add a medium for $6.50, making the large size look like a bargain.
- Subscriptions – “Basic” for $10 and “Premium” for $30. Then they add a “Standard” for $28, making $30 for Premium seem totally reasonable.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Spot the decoy – if one option is clearly worse but similar to another, it’s manipulation.
- Compare only the main options – ignore the extra choice designed to influence you.
- Make conscious decisions – if you’re being pushed toward something, ask yourself if it’s really the best choice.

title: Default Effect – when you stick with the pre-set option
description:
Do you leave checkboxes as they are when filling out a form? That’s Default Effect – the tendency to go with pre-set options, even if an alternative might be better.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Subscriptions – free trials automatically turn into paid plans unless you cancel.
- Retirement savings – in countries where people are auto-enrolled, participation rates are much higher.
- Privacy settings – websites pre-select “I agree to share my data,” and you don’t bother changing it.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Always check the settings – especially when something is already selected for you.
- Make intentional choices – convenience doesn’t always mean the best option.
- Ask ‘Who benefits from this?’ – if someone pre-selected an option, chances are it benefits them more than you.

title: Denomination Effect – when small bills disappear faster
description:
Is it easier to spend a handful of coins than a single large bill? That’s Denomination Effect – the tendency to spend money more easily when it’s in smaller denominations.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Cash spending – a $100 bill feels more valuable than the same amount in smaller notes, so it’s spent less often.
- Tipping – people find it easier to leave multiple small coins than a single large bill.
- Spending psychology – people make more impulsive purchases when paying with small denominations.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Carry large bills – it makes impulsive spending less tempting.
- Focus on total value, not form – coins and bills have the same purchasing power.
- Be mindful of ATM withdrawals – breaking large bills can be a subtle trick to make you spend more.

title: Distinction Bias – when differences seem bigger than they are
description:
Do two smartphones seem drastically different in a store, but once you buy one, the difference feels minimal? That’s Distinction Bias – the tendency to perceive differences as more significant when evaluating options side by side.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Shopping – a 5% screen brightness difference between laptops seems crucial, but in daily use, you wouldn’t notice.
- Job selection – two offers seem drastically different in small details, but months later, they feel similar.
- Technology – one smartphone loads 0.2 seconds faster, and it seems important, but in actual use, you wouldn’t care.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Evaluate each option on its own – ask yourself: if I only had one choice, would I be happy with it?
- Don’t obsess over minor differences – if the distinction isn’t noticeable in real life, it’s not worth stressing over.
- Remember that comparisons amplify differences – many distinctions fade once the decision is made.

title: Domain Neglect Bias – when you ignore relevant knowledge from other fields
description:
Do you think you can run a business without understanding human psychology? That’s Domain Neglect Bias – the tendency to ignore relevant knowledge from other fields when solving complex problems.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Business – launching a product without marketing, assuming a good product sells itself.
- Medicine – a doctor focuses only on symptoms, ignoring lifestyle factors.
- IT & Security – an engineer designs a secure system but forgets that users won’t follow complicated rules.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Think beyond your field – complex problems require interdisciplinary knowledge.
- Don’t dismiss related disciplines – every field offers valuable insights.
- Seek input from experts in other areas – sometimes, your problem has already been solved elsewhere.

title: Context Neglect Bias – when technology forgets about people
description:
Do you build complex systems without considering how real people will use them? That’s Context Neglect Bias – the tendency to solve technological challenges without accounting for human behavior and needs.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- IT & UX – a system is highly functional, but users struggle with its interface.
- Security – strong passwords protect accounts, but people write them down on sticky notes.
- AI & Automation – an algorithm makes decisions, but no one can explain its logic to users.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Put people at the center of decisions – technology should be useful, not just advanced.
- Test with real users – if a system works in theory but frustrates users, it’s a failure.
- Remember that humans aren’t machines – if your solution relies on perfect user behavior, it’s doomed.

title: Berkson’s Paradox – when two things seem connected, but they aren’t
description:
Does it seem like successful people are less kind because there aren’t many kind, successful people? That’s Berkson’s Paradox – a logical fallacy where an observed relationship between variables appears due to selection bias, not real causation.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Career & Personality – it seems like wealthy people are less kind, but kind, unsuccessful people just aren’t included in the sample.
- Hospitals – many COVID patients also have diabetes, but that doesn’t mean diabetes causes COVID – diabetics are just more likely to be hospitalized.
- College admissions – elite schools accept only top students, making it seem like there are no smart students with lower grades, when in fact, they just weren’t selected.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Watch for selection bias – not all groups are equally represented in the data.
- Check what actually causes the effect – sometimes, a connection appears simply due to how the data was collected.
- Don’t jump to conclusions – correlation does not imply causation.

title: Escalation of Commitment – when you keep investing despite clear failure
description:
Do you keep watching a boring movie just because you’ve already spent an hour on it? That’s Escalation of Commitment (Sunk Cost Fallacy) – the tendency to keep investing in a failing decision just because too much has already been put in.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Business – a company keeps pouring money into a failing project because “we’ve already invested too much to stop.”
- Relationships – people stay in unhappy relationships because “so many years have been spent.”
- Gambling & Entertainment – you keep playing, hoping to recover losses, but end up losing even more.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Re-evaluate the situation – past investments don’t matter, only future decisions do.
- Separate emotions from logic – sunk costs can’t be recovered, so they shouldn’t influence choices.
- Ask the right question – if you were starting fresh, would you still invest in this?

title: G.I. Joe Fallacy – when you think knowing a bias makes you immune to it
description:
Do you think that just knowing about cognitive biases makes you immune to them? That’s G.I. Joe Fallacy – the belief that awareness of a bias is enough to eliminate its effects. Unfortunately, self-control doesn’t work that way.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Financial decisions – even knowing about the ‘sunk cost fallacy,’ you still cling to bad investments.
- Productivity – you read books on time management but still procrastinate.
- Stereotypes – you understand that biases are bad, yet you still catch yourself making stereotypical judgments.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Practice, don’t just learn – recognizing a bias doesn’t mean you’ll stop falling for it.
- Build systems, don’t rely on willpower – if you know you’re prone to an error, set up safeguards against it.
- Stay humble – even the smartest people fall into cognitive traps.

title: Gambler’s Fallacy – when you think the past changes the future odds
description:
Do you think that after flipping five heads in a row, tails is ‘due’ to happen next? That’s Gambler’s Fallacy – the mistaken belief that past events influence future probabilities, even when each event is independent.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Gambling – believing that after a losing streak, you’re ‘bound’ to win soon.
- Lotteries – assuming a number that hasn’t come up in a while is ‘overdue.’
- Life decisions – thinking that after a series of bad events, good luck must finally arrive, even though the odds remain the same.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Understand that random events are independent – dice don’t ‘remember’ past rolls.
- Don’t look for patterns where there are none – long streaks don’t change probabilities.
- Use logic, not intuition – the likelihood of each event remains unchanged, no matter what happened before.

title: Hot-Hand Fallacy – when you think winning increases your chances of winning again
description:
Did you make three shots in a row and now feel like the fourth is more likely to go in? That’s Hot-Hand Fallacy – the belief that after a streak of success, your chances of continued success increase, even when events are random.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Sports – a basketball player makes three shots in a row, and everyone thinks he’s ‘on fire,’ even though each shot is independent.
- Gambling – a player wins multiple times and bets more, believing their ‘hot streak’ will continue.
- Investments – when stocks keep rising, people assume they’ll keep going up, but markets don’t work that way.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Remember that random events are independent – past success doesn’t change future probabilities.
- Don’t confuse skill with luck – if your success is based on skill, it might be predictable, but if it’s random, it’s not.
- Avoid overconfidence – winning before doesn’t guarantee winning again, especially in chance-based situations.

title: Plan Continuation Bias – when you stick to the plan even when the situation has changed
description:
Have you ever stuck to a route even after realizing there’s a shorter path? That’s Plan Continuation Bias – the tendency to stick to an initial plan, even when the situation has changed and it no longer makes sense.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Aviation – pilots continue landing in poor conditions when aborting would be safer.
- Projects – a team sticks to an outdated strategy despite new evidence showing it won’t work.
- Personal life – someone stays in an unfulfilling career or relationship just because they’ve ‘invested too much.’

💡 How to avoid it?
- Stay flexible – be willing to reassess plans as new information arises.
- Evaluate relevance – just because a plan was good at the start doesn’t mean it’s still the best option.
- Don’t be afraid to change course – admitting a mistake and adapting is always better than stubbornly heading into failure.

title: Subadditivity Effect – when parts seem more probable than the whole
description:
Do events seem more likely when broken into parts than when considered as a whole? That’s Subadditivity Effect – the tendency to judge the probability of separate components as higher than the probability of the entire event.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Weather forecasts – people think “30% chance of rain in the morning or 30% in the evening” means rain is more likely than the overall “50% chance of rain today.”
- Risk assessment – asking about the probability of a “terrorist attack at an airport,” “at a subway,” and “on a train” separately results in higher total perceived risk than asking about a “terrorist attack in the country.”
- Business evaluations – the likelihood of individual project stages succeeding seems higher than the probability of the entire project’s success.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Remember that parts can’t be more probable than the whole – if an event includes all options, its probability can’t be lower.
- Don’t trust fragmented forecasts without context – broken-down probabilities can distort perception.
- Double-check logical inconsistencies – if the sum of probabilities exceeds 100%, there’s an error in judgment.

title: Time-Saving Bias – when speed tricks your sense of time
description:
Do you think increasing speed from 80 to 100 km/h saves a lot of time, while 20 to 40 km/h barely makes a difference? That’s Time-Saving Bias – the tendency to overestimate time saved at high speeds and underestimate time saved at low speeds.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Driving – going from 20 to 40 km/h cuts travel time in half, but 100 to 120 km/h saves only a few minutes.
- Work processes – speeding up the final stage of a project seems like a major time saver, but the biggest gains were possible at the start.
- Sports & fitness – you believe a 5% speed boost matters most at peak performance, while ignoring that the biggest improvements happen early on.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Measure time savings in actual minutes – it’s not about how much faster you go, but how much time you truly save.
- Remember that efficiency gains are bigger at lower speeds – doubling speed at the start saves more time than a small increase at the end.
- Don’t chase illusionary improvements – small speed increases at high levels give minimal benefits but create a false sense of efficiency.

title: Zero-Sum Bias – when you think someone’s gain is your loss
description:
Do you think that if someone gets richer, others must get poorer? That’s Zero-Sum Bias – the mistaken belief that one person’s gain must come at another’s expense, even when resources can grow.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Economics – believing that if one country prospers, another must suffer, even though global wealth increases.
- Career – thinking a colleague’s promotion reduces your chances, even though the company could expand.
- Relationships – assuming a friend’s new connections mean they value you less, even though social circles can grow.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Remember that many resources grow – money, knowledge, opportunities, and relationships can expand rather than just shift around.
- Don’t view everything as competition – many situations create mutual benefits, not just winners and losers.
- Look at facts, not feelings – if someone succeeds, it doesn’t mean you’re worse off.

title: Ambiguity Effect – when you avoid the unknown, even if it might be better
description:
Do you avoid trying a new restaurant because there are no reviews, even though it might be better? That’s Ambiguity Effect – the tendency to avoid options where the probability of success is unknown, even if they could be better.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Investments – people prefer a low but predictable return over a higher-risk, potentially more profitable option.
- Job choices – candidates choose a stable but boring job over a startup with more growth potential.
- Travel – sticking to familiar destinations instead of exploring unknown places that might be amazing.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Remember that lack of information ≠ bad outcome – unknown doesn’t mean unsuccessful.
- Assess potential rewards – sometimes the risk of uncertainty is outweighed by possible benefits.
- Don’t cling to the familiar – the best opportunities might be where you haven’t looked yet.

title: Disposition Effect – when you sell winners but cling to losers
description:
Do you sell stocks that have gained value but hold onto losing ones, hoping they’ll recover? That’s Disposition Effect – the tendency to cash in on winners too early and hold onto losers for too long.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Investments – investors quickly sell profitable stocks but hesitate to cut losses on failing ones.
- Business – shutting down successful projects for quick gains while keeping failing ones alive.
- Personal life – staying in toxic relationships just because of the time already invested.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Base decisions on data, not emotions – if an asset is falling, ask yourself: would I buy it now?
- Focus on the future, not the past – losses are already incurred; the key is what to do next.
- Don’t be afraid to admit mistakes – the best way to minimize losses is to cut bad investments early.

title: Dread Aversion – when fearing the worst is worse than the event itself
description:
Do you stress over an upcoming exam more than you actually suffer during it? That’s Dread Aversion – the tendency to experience fear of an unpleasant event much more intensely than the pleasure of anticipating a good one.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Medicine – the fear of a painful procedure is worse than the procedure itself.
- Work – dreading an upcoming presentation or project drains more energy than actually doing it.
- Personal life – anxiety before a breakup or tough conversation is often worse than the conversation itself.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Recognize that anticipation is worse than reality – the fear before an event is usually stronger than the event itself.
- Don’t delay the inevitable – the sooner you face the challenge, the less time you spend worrying.
- Focus on facts, not imagination – the mind tends to exaggerate negative possibilities.

title: Endowment Effect – when what’s yours feels more valuable
description:
Would you sell something only for much more than you’d be willing to pay for it? That’s Endowment Effect – the tendency to overvalue things just because you own them.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Selling items – people demand more for things they own than they would pay for the same item.
- Business & negotiations – sellers believe their offers are worth more than buyers are willing to pay.
- Shopping – free trials make people feel ownership, making them less likely to return the product.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Assess items objectively – ask yourself if you’d buy it for the price you’re asking.
- Separate emotions from value – just owning something doesn’t make it worth more.
- Be wary of free trials – businesses know you’ll feel attached once you start using a product.

title: Loss Aversion – when losing hurts more than winning feels good
description:
Does losing $100 feel much worse than finding $100 feels good? That’s Loss Aversion – the tendency to feel losses more intensely than equivalent gains.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Investments – investors hold onto losing stocks to avoid ‘locking in’ losses, even when selling is the better move.
- Work & negotiations – people cling to bad deals just to ‘avoid losing,’ even if better options exist.
- Personal life – fear of ending relationships or quitting a job, even when they no longer bring happiness.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Look at the bigger picture – loss aversion can cloud rational decisions.
- Let go of what no longer benefits you – whether it’s a job, an investment, or a relationship.
- Remember that new opportunities outweigh old losses – closing one door often opens another.

title: Pseudocertainty Effect – when you avoid risk in gains but chase it in losses
description:
Do you prefer a guaranteed win but take risks to avoid losses? That’s Pseudocertainty Effect – the tendency to be cautious when things are good but take risks when things go bad.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Investments – you sell profitable assets too soon to ‘lock in gains’ but hold onto losing ones, hoping to recover.
- Health – you choose safe treatment when the prognosis is good but take risks when things get worse.
- Business – you opt for steady profits over new opportunities but take big risks to save a failing project.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Assess risks the same way in all situations – don’t fall into the trap of being cautious in success but reckless in failure.
- Don’t chase losses – if you’re already losing, making an emotional bet won’t fix it.
- Focus on long-term outcomes – don’t let fear or short-term thinking drive your decisions.

title: Status Quo Bias – when you resist change, even if it’s better
description:
Do you stick with your old phone even though a new one would be better? That’s Status Quo Bias – the tendency to resist change and keep things as they are, even when change would be beneficial.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Finances – you don’t switch banks or plans because “it’s fine,” even if you’d save money.
- Career – you stay in a boring job just because it’s familiar, even though better options exist.
- Relationships – you stay in an unfulfilling relationship just because it’s been going on for years.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Consider the benefits of change – the new option might be better, even if switching is uncomfortable.
- Don’t mistake familiarity for the best choice – just because it’s known doesn’t mean it’s optimal.
- Give yourself a chance to upgrade – try new things before automatically rejecting them.

title: System Justification – when you defend the system, even if it harms you
description:
Do you believe that if something has been around for a long time, it must be good? That’s System Justification – the tendency to defend the status quo, even when it’s unfair or personally harmful.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Economy – people justify low wages and harsh working conditions because “that’s how it has always been.”
- Politics – voters support the same leaders, even if they bring no change, out of fear that alternatives might be worse.
- Social norms – discrimination or injustice gets defended simply because “that’s just how the world works.”

💡 How to avoid it?
- Ask: “Who benefits from this?” – could the system be improved?
- Don’t fear change – just because something is old doesn’t mean it’s right.
- Look at facts, not traditions – systems often sustain themselves even when they no longer serve people well.

title: Dunning–Kruger Effect – when the less you know, the more confident you are
description:
Does a beginner confidently explain a complex topic while an expert hesitates? That’s Dunning–Kruger Effect – the tendency for incompetent people to overestimate themselves, while true experts underestimate their knowledge.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Work – a rookie thinks a task will take a day, while an experienced professional knows the real challenges and sets realistic deadlines.
- Politics & social media – someone with no expertise easily gives opinions on economics, medicine, and science, while real experts are cautious in their statements.
- Learning – a beginner believes they understand a topic after one lecture, while a scientist knows that the more you learn, the more questions arise.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Be wary of oversimplified conclusions – if something seems too easy, you might be missing the full picture.
- Don’t be afraid to admit knowledge gaps – true professionals understand how complex things really are.
- Listen to experts, not just the loudest voices – confidence doesn’t equal competence.

title: Hot-Cold Empathy Gap – when you underestimate how emotions will change your choices
description:
Do you believe you'll always eat healthy, but then grab fast food when hungry? That’s Hot-Cold Empathy Gap – the tendency to underestimate how emotions, fatigue, or cravings will influence your behavior.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Dieting – you think you’ll avoid sweets, but when stressed, you reach for chocolate.
- Finances – you plan to save money, but in the store, emotions take over and you make impulse purchases.
- Conflicts – you promise to stay calm, but in the moment, anger takes control, and you say things you regret.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Acknowledge emotional influence – expect hunger, stress, or exhaustion to change your decisions.
- Create barriers – don’t carry your card if you want to avoid impulse spending, or keep junk food out of the house.
- Be honest with yourself – ask: will I really resist in the moment, or am I just hoping I will?

title: Hard–Easy Effect – when hard tasks seem easier and easy tasks seem harder
description:
Do you think you’ll learn a new language in a month but doubt you can pass a simple test? That’s Hard–Easy Effect – the tendency to overestimate performance on hard tasks and underestimate it on easy ones.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Learning – you assume you’ll ace a tough exam but make mistakes on simple questions.
- Work – you take on a big project with enthusiasm but put off small tasks, thinking they’ll take more time than they actually do.
- Sports – you’re confident about running a marathon but underestimate the importance of basic warm-ups.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Assess tasks objectively – easy doesn’t mean unimportant, and hard doesn’t always mean quick.
- Don’t trust first impressions – if a task seems easy, check for hidden challenges.
- Track your predictions – notice when you overestimate hard things and underestimate easy ones.

title: Illusion of Explanatory Depth – when you think you understand until you have to explain
description:
Do you think you understand how a fridge works but struggle to explain what happens inside? That’s Illusion of Explanatory Depth – the tendency to overestimate your knowledge of a topic until you actually have to explain it.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Technology – you believe you know how Wi-Fi works but get confused when trying to explain it.
- Economics & Politics – you’re sure you can describe inflation, but beyond a few phrases, your understanding is shallow.
- Medicine – you know vaccines are beneficial but can’t explain how they function.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Try explaining in simple terms – if you can’t explain it to a 5-year-old, you don’t fully understand it.
- Be ready for questions – check if you can answer follow-ups rather than just repeating memorized statements.
- Develop real understanding – don’t stop at surface-level knowledge; dig deeper into the details.

title: Impostor Syndrome – when you fear being ‘exposed’ as a fraud
description:
Do you achieve success but still feel like you're just faking it? That’s Impostor Syndrome – the tendency to downplay your achievements and fear that others will soon ‘expose’ you as incompetent.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Work – you get a promotion but believe it was a mistake, and that soon everyone will realize you’re ‘not good enough.’
- Education – you pass exams but think it was just luck rather than your actual knowledge.
- Creative fields – even with recognition and success, you feel like your ideas ‘aren’t that great’ and people will figure it out soon.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Remember that success isn’t just luck – if you achieved something, it’s because of your efforts.
- Compare yourself to real standards, not perfection – everyone makes mistakes, but that doesn’t make them impostors.
- Accept compliments and recognition – if people value your work, it means you’re actually good at it.

title: Objectivity Illusion – when you believe you’re unbiased, unlike everyone else
description:
Do you believe you see things as they truly are, while others are biased? That’s Objectivity Illusion – the tendency to think you’re rational and unbiased, but only notice cognitive errors in others.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Discussions & debates – you assume your arguments are logical while your opponent is emotional, even when the opposite is true.
- Politics & news – you think you see the ‘real picture’ while others are victims of propaganda.
- Work & management – you believe your decisions are objective, while colleagues are driven by personal biases.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Remember that no one is fully objective – including you.
- Listen to other perspectives – disagreement doesn’t automatically mean the other person is wrong.
- Question yourself – what if my view is also influenced by biases?

title: Belief Bias – when you judge logic based on whether you agree with the conclusion
description:
Do you only find arguments convincing when their conclusion aligns with your beliefs? That’s Belief Bias – the tendency to judge an argument’s strength based on how believable its conclusion seems, rather than its actual logic.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Debates & discussions – you reject a logically valid argument because its conclusion contradicts your views.
- Politics & news – you accept weak arguments if they support your beliefs and dismiss strong ones if they challenge them.
- Science & research – you trust a study because it confirms your opinion but reject another, even if it’s more rigorous, because it contradicts you.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Evaluate logic, not just the conclusion – if an argument is logically sound, it’s strong regardless of your opinion.
- Check your reactions – if you instinctively reject something, ask yourself: is this logical?
- Be open to changing your mind – if the evidence contradicts your beliefs, maybe it’s time to reconsider them.

title: Illusory Truth Effect – when repeated lies start to feel like truth
description:
