Do statements seem more true the more you hear them? That’s Illusory Truth Effect – the tendency to believe information simply because it’s familiar or easy to process.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Fake news & propaganda – false facts start feeling true when they’re repeated often enough.
- Marketing & advertising – slogans like “natural product” create an illusion of healthiness, even when it’s not true.
- Social media – posts with many likes and shares feel more credible, even if they lack facts.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Check sources, not just frequency – just because something sounds familiar doesn’t make it true.
- Be skeptical of repeated claims – if a phrase is everywhere, that doesn’t mean it’s accurate.
- Don’t trust ease of understanding – easy to process ≠ correct.

title: Rhyme as Reason Effect – when something feels true just because it rhymes
description:
Do phrases like ‘If the glove doesn’t fit, you must acquit’ sound more convincing just because they rhyme? That’s Rhyme as Reason Effect – the tendency to perceive rhyming statements as more truthful, even when they lack substance.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Court cases – defense lawyers use catchy rhymes to sway juries (‘If it doesn’t fit, you must acquit’).
- Politics & propaganda – rhyming slogans are easier to remember and create an illusion of truth.
- Advertising & marketing – phrases like ‘Red Bull gives you wings’ feel more persuasive than dry facts.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Focus on meaning, not just wording – truth isn’t determined by how catchy a phrase is.
- Be cautious with rhyming slogans – they stick in your mind, but that doesn’t make them accurate.
- Analyze the argument – if something sounds convincing, check if there’s real logic behind it.

title: Subjective Validation – when something feels true because you want it to be
description:
Do you read a horoscope and think, ‘That’s so me!’? That’s Subjective Validation – the tendency to believe information is true if it aligns with your beliefs or desires, even if it’s vague or coincidental.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Horoscopes & predictions – generic statements seem accurate because we interpret them to fit ourselves.
- Coincidences – you connect unrelated events simply because they seem meaningful.
- Conspiracy theories – you find ‘proof’ for what you already believe while ignoring contradicting evidence.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Look for objective evidence – truth doesn’t depend on whether you want it to be true.
- Don’t trust everything that ‘feels right’ – just because something ‘fits’ doesn’t mean it’s real.
- Question yourself – if something seems convincing, ask: is there actual proof?

title: Action Bias – when taking action feels better than doing nothing
description:
Do you feel the need to take action, even when waiting would be smarter? That’s Action Bias – the tendency to act in any situation, even when inaction would be more effective.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Sports – goalkeepers dive during penalties, even though statistics show staying put is often better.
- Finance – traders make moves just to ‘do something,’ even when the market calls for patience.
- Management – leaders introduce new processes and changes, even when things are working fine.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Ask if the action adds real value – sometimes the best move is no move at all.
- Don’t act just for the sake of action – impulsive decisions often do more harm than good.
- Remember that inaction is a strategy too – sometimes waiting and observing is the smartest choice.

title: Additive Bias – when you add instead of subtracting
description:
Do you think improving something always means adding more? That’s Additive Bias – the tendency to solve problems by adding new elements, even when removing something would work better.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Design & UI – instead of simplifying a product, companies add more buttons and features, making it worse.
- Laws & regulations – new rules keep piling up, but outdated ones are never removed, creating inefficiency.
- Management – to increase productivity, companies introduce more processes and reports instead of cutting bureaucracy.

💡 How to avoid it?
- First, ask what can be removed – problems are often solved by subtracting, not adding.
- Simplicity = efficiency – the less clutter, the better a system works.
- Don’t overcomplicate things – not everything needs more features; sometimes, less is more.

title: Attribute Substitution – when your brain picks an easy answer instead of the right one
description:
When faced with a complex question, your brain might unknowingly replace it with an easier one. That’s Attribute Substitution – the tendency to answer a simpler question instead of the actual, more difficult one.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Probability estimation – instead of calculating real odds, we judge based on how easily an example comes to mind.
- Politics & news – complex economic issues get reduced to a catchy emotional slogan.
- Personal perception – we judge people not by their real abilities but by first impressions.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Notice when a question seems too easy – your brain might be simplifying it without you realizing.
- Check what you’re really answering – does your response actually match the original question?
- Think slower – difficult questions require conscious analysis, not quick intuitive answers.

title: Curse of Knowledge – when you forget what it’s like to be a beginner
description:
Do you struggle to explain something in simple terms because it’s obvious to you? That’s Curse of Knowledge – a cognitive bias where knowledgeable people find it hard to see things from the perspective of those who don’t know.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Teaching & mentoring – experts explain complex topics assuming everyone already knows the basics.
- Work & management – leaders give vague instructions, forgetting that employees have less context.
- Communication – technical experts speak in jargon, leaving others confused.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Remember that others don’t see the world as you do – simplify explanations.
- Test your explanations – if a beginner doesn’t understand, the problem is in your delivery.
- Use examples and analogies – they make complex ideas easier to grasp.

title: Declinism – when the past seems golden, and the future looks bleak
description:
Do you think the past was better, people were kinder, and life was simpler? That’s Declinism – the tendency to romanticize the past and believe the future will only get worse.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Society & politics – ‘People used to be honest, but now the world is falling apart.’
- Technology – ‘Things were built to last, now everything is disposable.’
- Personal life – ‘The best years are behind me, the future looks grim.’

💡 How to avoid it?
- Remember that memory distorts reality – we recall the good from the past and exaggerate future problems.
- Compare using facts, not nostalgia – real progress often proves otherwise.
- Focus on opportunities, not fears – the future can be bright if viewed without bias.

title: End-of-History Illusion – when you think you won’t change anymore
description:
Do you think you’ve reached your final form and won’t change much in the future? That’s End-of-History Illusion – the belief that you will stay the same, even though you’ve changed a lot in the past.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Personal growth – you believe your tastes, values, and views will stay the same, but in 10 years, you’ll look back and barely recognize yourself.
- Future planning – you assume your needs in five years will be the same as today, forgetting how much they’ve changed in the past five.
- Relationships & career – you make long-term commitments based on today’s preferences, not realizing they might shift.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Accept that change is inevitable – you’ve changed before, and you will change again.
- Leave room for flexibility – decisions that feel right now might not in the future.
- Don’t limit yourself – if something doesn’t appeal to you today, that doesn’t mean you won’t want it in 10 years.

title: Exaggerated Expectation – when reality is always less extreme than you imagined
description:
Did you expect a disaster, but nothing happened? Or thought something would change your life, but it turned out underwhelming? That’s Exaggerated Expectation – the tendency to predict more extreme outcomes than what actually occurs.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Financial markets – expecting sudden booms or crashes, when in reality, changes are gradual.
- Politics & global events – believing that one decision will ‘change everything,’ but life continues as usual.
- Personal life – thinking a move or new job will instantly make you happy, but real change takes time.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Review past predictions – how often did your extreme expectations come true?
- Be realistic – most change happens gradually, not all at once.
- Don’t dramatize the future – reality is usually less extreme than our fears or hopes.

title: Form-Function Attribution Bias – when you judge a robot by its looks, not its abilities
description:
Do you see a cute robot and assume it’s smart and friendly? Or if it looks mechanical, do you think it’s incapable? That’s Form-Function Attribution Bias – the tendency to judge a robot’s abilities based on appearance rather than actual functionality.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Humanoid robots – if a robot has a face, people expect it to understand emotions, even if it’s just a toy.
- Minimalist design – if a robot looks basic and technical, people underestimate its capabilities, even if it’s highly advanced.
- Voice assistants – if a system speaks naturally, people assume it ‘understands’ them, even though it’s just a well-tuned algorithm.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Focus on real functions – a robot’s appearance doesn’t determine its intelligence.
- Don’t expect human emotions from machines – a friendly face doesn’t mean a robot is self-aware.
- Learn about technology – understanding AI limitations helps prevent false expectations.

title: Fundamental Pain Bias – when your pain is real, but others’ seem exaggerated
description:
Do you believe your pain is real and objective, but others are just exaggerating? That’s Fundamental Pain Bias – the tendency to believe you report your own pain accurately while assuming others overstate theirs.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Medicine – patients feel doctors don’t take their pain seriously, yet they dismiss others’ complaints as overblown.
- Work & sports – you think your exhaustion is legitimate, but when a colleague or teammate complains, it seems like they’re just whining.
- Relationships – you see your emotions and struggles as valid but view others’ as ‘too dramatic.’

💡 How to avoid it?
- Remember that others’ pain is just as real as yours – it’s just harder to feel someone else’s discomfort.
- Don’t compare subjective experiences – pain levels differ between people in the same situation.
- Practice empathy – respect others’ feelings, even if they seem exaggerated to you.

title: Hedonic Recall Bias – when satisfied employees think they earn more, and unhappy ones think they earn less
description:
Do you feel satisfied with your salary and think you earn more than you actually do? Or, if you're unhappy, does your salary seem smaller than it really is? That’s Hedonic Recall Bias – the tendency to overestimate or underestimate earnings based on job satisfaction.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Salary negotiations – satisfied employees might ask for less than they could because they believe they already earn a lot.
- Perceived unfairness – dissatisfied employees tend to feel their salary is even lower than it actually is.
- Financial planning – misjudging income can lead to poor financial decisions.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Look at actual numbers, not feelings – check your payslip instead of relying on memory.
- Separate emotions from finances – job satisfaction doesn’t change your actual earnings.
- Reevaluate your market value – even if you’re happy with your salary, check what similar jobs pay.

title: Hindsight Bias – when the past looks obvious in retrospect
description:
Do past events seem obvious in hindsight? That’s Hindsight Bias – the tendency to see past events as more predictable than they actually were.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Financial markets – after a crash, people say ‘it was obvious,’ even though no one accurately predicted it before.
- Sports & betting – after a game, the winner seems ‘predictable,’ but before the match, it was uncertain.
- Personal life – after a breakup, you think ‘the signs were clear,’ even though you missed them before.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Remember that predictions work forward, not backward – just because something seems obvious now doesn’t mean it was before.
- Track your actual predictions – write down your thoughts beforehand to avoid the illusion of ‘I always knew it.’
- Be honest with yourself – if it was so predictable, you would have acted differently.

title: Impact Bias – when you overestimate how long or intense your emotions will be
description:
Do you think winning the lottery will make you happy forever? Or that a failure will leave you devastated for months? That’s Impact Bias – the tendency to overestimate the intensity and duration of future emotions.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Financial success – you believe a higher salary or a luxury purchase will bring lasting happiness, but the excitement fades quickly.
- Failures & disappointments – you expect a failed exam or breakup to ruin you, but after a few weeks, emotions subside.
- Life changes – moving to a new city or starting a new job feels life-changing, but within months, it becomes normal.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Remember that emotions don’t last forever – happiness and sadness fade faster than you expect.
- Don’t overestimate the impact of events – you adapt better than you think.
- Make decisions wisely – don’t assume your emotions will stay the same forever.

title: Information Bias – when you seek information that won’t change your decision
description:
Do you believe more information always leads to better decisions? That’s Information Bias – the tendency to seek data even when it won’t impact your choice or actions.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Medicine – patients demand extra tests even when the diagnosis is already clear.
- Work & management – companies collect endless reports that no one actually uses for decision-making.
- Personal life – you read hundreds of reviews before buying something, but in the end, you choose based on first impressions.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Ask: will this change my decision? – if not, you don’t need the data.
- Don’t confuse quantity with value – more information creates noise, not clarity.
- Act instead of overanalyzing – knowledge without action is wasted time.

title: Hungry Judge Effect – when your body makes decisions for you
description:
Do you feel the world is more frustrating when you're hungry or tired? That’s Hungry Judge Effect – the tendency to judge situations more harshly or leniently depending on your physical state.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Legal decisions – studies show that judges give harsher sentences before lunch and more lenient ones after eating.
- Work & negotiations – a tired manager is more likely to reject an offer they would accept when well-rested.
- Personal life – small conflicts with a partner seem worse when you’re hungry or sleep-deprived.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Check your state before big decisions – hunger, fatigue, and stress distort judgment.
- Don’t decide on impulse – if you’re irritated, delay the decision and revisit it later.
- Ask yourself if the problem is real – maybe it’s not the situation, but your physical state affecting perception.

title: Money Illusion – when a bigger number feels like more money
description:
Do you feel richer when your salary increases, even if prices rise even faster? That’s Money Illusion – the tendency to focus on the nominal value of money rather than its actual purchasing power.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Salaries & inflation – people celebrate pay raises without realizing inflation eats up the gains.
- Currency exchange – 1000 local units seem like more than 100 dollars, even if their value is the same.
- Investments – nominal capital growth can be misleading if inflation isn’t considered.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Focus on real purchasing power – what matters is what your money can actually buy.
- Track inflation – a higher income doesn’t always mean a higher standard of living.
- Don’t be fooled by big numbers – understand what your money is truly worth in the long run.

title: Moral Credential Effect – when doing good gives you a pass to do bad
description:
Do you feel like one good deed gives you a free pass for less ethical behavior? That’s Moral Credential Effect – the tendency to believe that doing good earns you the right to be less moral in the future.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Ethics & honesty – someone who donates to charity may feel justified in bending tax rules.
- Diet & health – after a workout, you ‘reward’ yourself with unhealthy food.
- Social behavior – after helping a colleague, you might ignore their next request, feeling like you’ve ‘done enough.’

💡 How to avoid it?
- Don’t use past good deeds as an excuse – being good before doesn’t make bad behavior okay.
- Track consistency in your actions – judge yourself by patterns, not single moments.
- Separate good deeds from indulgences – doing good shouldn’t grant you a ‘moral free pass.’

title: Non-Adaptive Choice Switching – when one bad experience makes you avoid a good choice
description:
Did you make the right decision, but due to bad luck, you now refuse to make it again? That’s Non-Adaptive Choice Switching – the tendency to avoid an optimal choice after one bad outcome.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Finance & investing – an investor loses money on a solid stock during a downturn and avoids investing in promising companies ever again.
- Relationships – after one bad date, someone refuses to meet similar partners, even if they are a great match.
- Work & career – after failing once on a new project, an employee avoids similar tasks out of fear.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Separate luck from decision quality – even the best choices sometimes lead to bad results.
- Analyze the reasons – was the mistake in the decision itself or just random bad luck?
- Don’t let one bad experience create irrational fear – past failure doesn’t mean future failure.

title: Mere Exposure Effect – when you like something just because it’s familiar
description:
Have you noticed that the more you see something, the more you like it? That’s Mere Exposure Effect – the tendency to prefer things just because they are familiar.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Advertising & brands – the more you see a logo or slogan, the more trustworthy it seems.
- Music & culture – a song you disliked at first suddenly becomes your favorite after hearing it a few times.
- People & relationships – a colleague or acquaintance seems more likable simply because you see them often.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Recognize the power of exposure – just because you’re used to something doesn’t mean it’s the best option.
- Don’t mistake familiarity for quality – evaluate things objectively, not just based on how often you encounter them.
- Expand your choices – try new products, music, and connections to avoid getting stuck in the exposure trap.

title: Omission Bias – when doing nothing feels safer than making a mistake
description:
Do you believe that doing nothing is safer, even if it leads to bad outcomes? That’s Omission Bias – the tendency to view harmful actions as worse than equally harmful inactions.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Medicine – parents avoid vaccines due to fear of side effects, even though the risks of not vaccinating are greater.
- Work & management – leaders refuse to make tough decisions out of fear of mistakes, leading to bigger failures.
- Ethics & morality – people criticize a doctor for prescribing the wrong drug but ignore the harm of not treating a patient at all.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Consider the cost of inaction – doing nothing is still a choice with real consequences.
- Don’t let fear of mistakes freeze you – sometimes action is better than passive waiting.
- Be honest with yourself – avoiding responsibility doesn’t make you less accountable for the outcome.

title: Optimism Bias – when you believe things will go well, even if the odds say otherwise
description:
Do you believe bad things happen to others, but not to you? That’s Optimism Bias – the tendency to underestimate negative events and overestimate positive outcomes.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Finance & investments – people believe their business will succeed, even when statistics suggest otherwise.
- Health & safety – drivers assume they won’t get into accidents and ignore precautions.
- Personal life – people think they will never divorce, despite high divorce rates.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Be realistic – hope for the best, but acknowledge risks.
- Trust data, not just gut feelings – if 90% of startups fail, yours isn’t immune.
- Plan for worst-case scenarios – anticipating problems isn’t pessimism, it’s smart thinking.

title: Ostrich Effect – when you ignore a problem, hoping it will go away
description:
Do you avoid checking your bank balance because you’re afraid of what you’ll see? That’s Ostrich Effect – the tendency to ignore negative information to avoid discomfort.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Finances – investors avoid looking at their portfolio during downturns to escape seeing losses.
- Health – people delay doctor visits despite alarming symptoms.
- Work & problems – difficult conversations get postponed in the hope that issues resolve themselves.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Problems don’t disappear when ignored – in fact, they usually get worse.
- The sooner you face reality, the more options you have – avoidance limits your ability to act.
- Ask yourself: ‘What’s the worst that can happen?’ – often, the truth is less scary than imagined.

title: Outcome Bias – when you judge a decision by its result, not its quality
description:
Do you think a decision was good just because it led to a positive outcome? That’s Outcome Bias – the tendency to judge the quality of a decision based on its final result rather than the logic behind it.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Finance – an investor takes a reckless bet, wins, and believes it was a ‘smart’ decision, ignoring the risk.
- Medicine – a doctor misdiagnoses a patient, but they recover anyway, making the treatment seem successful.
- Business & career – someone picks a strategy by luck, it works, and they now believe they always make the right calls.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Evaluate the process, not just the result – good decisions can lead to bad outcomes, and vice versa.
- Understand what really caused success or failure – was it skill, or just luck?
- Be honest with yourself – if a bad decision led to a good outcome, that doesn’t make it a good decision.

title: Pessimism Bias – when you believe everything will go wrong
description:
Do you always expect the worst, even when there’s no real reason to? That’s Pessimism Bias – the tendency to overestimate the likelihood of negative events, especially in people prone to depression.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Finance – fearing failure, someone avoids investing or starting a business, even when success is likely.
- Relationships – expecting betrayal or abandonment leads to unnecessary anxiety.
- Career & work – fear of failure stops people from taking new opportunities, even when risks are low.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Assess real probabilities – use facts, not emotions, to predict outcomes.
- Notice positive results – pessimists tend to overlook successful cases.
- Balance caution with action – considering risks is smart, but don’t let fear dictate your decisions.

title: Present Bias – when you choose instant rewards over long-term benefits
description:
Do you think, ‘Better a little now than more later’? That’s Present Bias – the tendency to overvalue short-term rewards and underestimate long-term consequences.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Finance – spending money immediately instead of saving or investing.
- Health – choosing fast food over healthy meals because it’s quicker and tastier.
- Study & work – procrastinating because relaxation now feels more important than future success.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Think like your future self – imagine yourself a year from now: what decision would they prefer?
- Create barriers to impulsive choices – use a 24-hour rule before making unplanned purchases.
- Focus on long-term benefits – remind yourself that small steps now lead to big results later.

title: Plant Blindness – when you fail to notice the green world around you
description:
Do you notice animals, buildings, and cars but overlook trees and flowers? That’s Plant Blindness – the tendency to ignore plants in the environment and underestimate their importance to life on Earth.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Cities without nature – people don’t realize how crucial urban trees are for clean air and climate regulation.
- Undervaluing plants – most people can name more car brands than tree species.
- Ecological apathy – by ignoring plants, people fail to see their role in ecosystems and why they need protection.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Start noticing the green world – consciously pay attention to trees, flowers, and their diversity.
- Learn about plants – make an effort to remember the names of new species you encounter.
- Understand their value – without plants, there would be no oxygen, food, or ecosystem to sustain us.

title: Prevention Bias – when prevention feels more valuable than response
description:
Do you believe it’s better to invest in preventing problems than detecting and responding to them? That’s Prevention Bias – the tendency to overvalue prevention, even when detection and response are equally effective.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Healthcare – society heavily funds vaccination but underestimates the importance of early disease detection.
- Business & cybersecurity – companies spend millions on preventing cyberattacks but neglect rapid incident response.
- Personal life – people try to eliminate all risks (e.g., over-insuring everything) but fail to plan how to handle problems when they arise.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Balance your approach – don’t just prevent; be ready to respond.
- Evaluate real risks – sometimes, detection and fast reaction matter more than trying to eliminate every possible risk.
- Think rationally about investments – if a dollar spent on response provides as much security as a dollar spent on prevention, don’t ignore response.

title: Probability Matching – when you guess instead of picking the best option
description:
Do you spread your choices across different options, even when one is clearly better? That’s Probability Matching – the tendency to match choices to probabilities instead of always picking the best option.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Gambling – players bet on multiple numbers instead of always choosing the most probable one.
- Business decisions – companies invest in multiple strategies even when one clearly outperforms the others.
- Personal behavior – people vary their actions when one approach consistently yields better results.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Pick the best, don’t guess – if one choice is objectively superior, stick with it.
- Don’t mistake probability for strategy – just because something happens occasionally doesn’t mean it’s worth betting on.
- Trust the math – when data shows one strategy wins more often, follow it.

title: Pro-Innovation Bias – when new technology seems perfect, and flaws are ignored
description:
Do you believe every new technology is the future while ignoring its flaws? That’s Pro-Innovation Bias – the tendency to overestimate the benefits of innovations while underestimating their limitations.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Cryptocurrency & blockchain – once seen as the future of finance, but many projects turned into speculation.
- Artificial intelligence – promised to automate everything, yet AI models still make critical errors.
- Medicine & biotech – new drugs are marketed as breakthroughs, but their long-term side effects are often unknown.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Find balance – new technology can be great, but it’s never perfect.
- Analyze risks – if something sounds too good to be true, it probably has hidden downsides.
- Wait for real-world results – before jumping on the hype train, see how it actually performs in practice.

title: Projection Bias – when you assume your future self will want what you want now
description:
Do you think your future self will have the same preferences, habits, and values as you do now? That’s Projection Bias – the tendency to overestimate how much your future self will align with your current desires.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Purchases – people buy yearly gym memberships, assuming they’ll stay motivated just as they feel today.
- Career choices – a ‘dream job’ may seem perfect now, but interests and passions evolve over time.
- Relationships – assuming the excitement of a new relationship will last forever, without considering natural changes.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Remember, you change over time – your views, tastes, and desires evolve.
- Set flexible goals – plan with the expectation that priorities may shift.
- Reflect on past changes – think about how your preferences have shifted over the last 5–10 years and apply that insight.

title: Proportionality Bias – when big events must have big causes
description:
Do you struggle to believe that major events can happen by chance? That’s Proportionality Bias – the tendency to assume that big events must have equally big causes, even when they don’t.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Conspiracy theories – people believe global crises or disasters are orchestrated by hidden forces rather than being random or due to human error.
- History & politics – assuming assassinations or revolutions are always part of a grand conspiracy rather than chaotic events.
- Medicine & science – seeking complex explanations for diseases and epidemics while dismissing simple scientific facts.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Remember, the world is chaotic – not everything has a hidden meaning or massive cause.
- Look for real evidence – rather than just what ‘sounds logical.’
- Don’t overcomplicate things – sometimes, the simplest explanation is the right one.

title: Recency Illusion – when you think something is new just because you recently noticed it
description:
Have you recently noticed a word, trend, or idea and assumed it’s brand new? That’s Recency Illusion – the tendency to believe something is new just because you’ve only recently become aware of it, even if it has existed for decades or centuries.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Language & words – thinking a slang term is brand new, when in reality, it has been used for decades.
- Cultural trends – assuming a concept is recent just because people around you started talking about it.
- Science & technology – believing an idea is revolutionary, when it’s actually based on older theories and discoveries.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Check the history of the phenomenon – before assuming something is new, research when it actually emerged.
- Don’t confuse personal discovery with actual innovation – just because you noticed it now doesn’t mean it’s recent.
- Be skeptical of media ‘new trends’ – many things are marketed as ‘new’ even when they’ve been around for years.

title: Systematic Bias – when errors in judgment follow a predictable pattern
description:
Do you think your decisions are objective, but they follow a recurring pattern of errors? That’s Systematic Bias – when deviations in judgment or data are not random but follow a predictable trend.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Science & research – if a measurement method consistently overestimates or underestimates results, the data becomes systematically biased.
- Business & forecasting – companies may repeatedly overestimate sales or underestimate expenses due to the same calculation errors.
- Personal life – people may systematically overrate their own abilities or underestimate others’ achievements.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Look for recurring errors – if deviations aren’t random, they might be a sign of systematic bias.
- Check your evaluation methods – often, the issue isn’t the data but how it’s collected or interpreted.
- Compare with independent sources – if different methods give different results, your evaluation system might be biased.

title: Peltzman Effect – when feeling safe makes you take more risks
description:
Do you act more recklessly when you feel safe, even though the risk remains? That’s Peltzman Effect – the tendency to offset increased safety by engaging in riskier behavior.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Driving – people drive more aggressively in cars with advanced safety features than in older models.
- Sports & outdoor activities – skiers or cyclists go faster when wearing protective gear, assuming it will save them.
- Finance – investors take bigger risks when they believe their losses are insured.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Safety doesn’t make you invincible – protection reduces risk but doesn’t eliminate it.
- Monitor your behavior – don’t let a sense of security lead to reckless decisions.
- Think about consequences – if you’re taking bigger risks because of added safety, ask yourself if it’s really worth it.

title: Surrogation – when the metric becomes more important than the goal
description:
Do you focus so much on numbers that you forget what they represent? That’s Surrogation – the tendency to mistake a metric for the actual goal, leading people to optimize the measure rather than achieving real success.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Business & sales – companies chase KPIs instead of genuinely improving service, leading to great numbers but unhappy customers.
- Education – students aim for high grades rather than true learning.
- Fitness & health – people focus on the number on the scale rather than their actual well-being.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Remember that metrics are just tools – what matters is the real outcome, not just the number.
- Ask yourself: what’s behind this? – are you achieving real progress or just ‘gaming’ the metric?
- Reality-check your progress – if the metric improves but nothing changes, you’ve fallen into the trap.

title: Teleological Bias – when you see purpose where there is none
description:
Do you believe everything happens for a reason? That’s Teleological Bias – the tendency to assign purpose or intention to events and objects, even when they arise randomly or without deliberate design.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Natural events – people think hurricanes, earthquakes, or pandemics happen ‘for a reason.’
- Evolution & biology – assuming everything in nature was ‘designed for something’ when evolution is a process of random selection.
- Personal life – believing failures or successes occur due to fate rather than chance or patterns.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Separate cause from purpose – just because something has a cause doesn’t mean it has intent or meaning.
- Think in probabilities, not destiny – many things happen randomly, without any specific plan.
- Be skeptical of patterns – if everything seems meaningful, check if you’re the one creating that meaning.

title: Turkey Illusion – when you assume stability until disaster strikes
description:
Do you assume things will stay the same just because they’ve always been stable? That’s Turkey Illusion – the tendency to ignore the risk of sudden change just because the past has been smooth.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Financial markets – investors believe stocks will keep rising until a sudden crash wipes out gains.
- Business & careers – companies and employees assume success will last forever, until an unexpected failure.
- Politics & society – people don’t expect crises or revolutions until they suddenly happen.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Remember that stability isn’t a guarantee – past success doesn’t mean the future is secure.
- Assess risks even when they seem invisible – disasters often build up slowly before striking suddenly.
- Be prepared for surprises – history shows that the unexpected is always just around the corner.

title: Unit Bias – when you consume everything just because it’s the ‘right’ portion
description:
Do you think a portion is the ‘right amount’ just because it’s served that way? That’s Unit Bias – the tendency to assume a standard serving size is ideal, even when it’s not.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Food & drinks – people finish meals even when full because ‘that’s the portion size.’
- Medicine – patients take a full pill even if half is enough to work.
- Work & productivity – employees assume they must be productive for a full 8-hour shift just because it’s the standard.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Listen to your body & logic – a standard portion doesn’t mean it’s right for you.
- Don’t follow patterns blindly – sometimes less is better, sometimes more is needed.
- Optimize consumption – whether it’s food, time, or resources, adjust to actual needs.

title: Value Selection Bias – when you cling to numbers even when they don’t apply
description:
Do you use numbers in a new context just because they exist? That’s Value Selection Bias – the tendency to rely on available numerical data even when logical reasoning or recalculation is needed.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Finance – investors assess opportunities based on outdated prices instead of current market conditions.
- Business analytics – managers rely on last year’s performance metrics, ignoring recent market shifts.
- Personal life – travelers plan trips based on old cost estimates and outdated weather reports.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Ask if the data is still relevant – past numbers might not apply to the present situation.
- Don’t trust numbers blindly – check if they actually fit the context.
- Remember that calculations change – new conditions require fresh evaluations, not old assumptions.

title: Weber–Fechner Law – when small differences in big numbers go unnoticed
description:
Can you tell the difference between 1 kg and 2 kg, but not between 101 kg and 102 kg? That’s Weber–Fechner Law – the difficulty in noticing small changes when dealing with large quantities.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Finance – a $10 difference feels huge on a $50 purchase but insignificant on a $10,000 deal.
- Weight & perception – gaining 1 kg is noticeable on a slim person but almost invisible at 150 kg.
- Sound & light – a small increase in volume is obvious in silence but hard to detect in a noisy environment.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Check percentage changes – absolute numbers can be misleading; percentages show the real impact.
- Don’t dismiss small differences – minor variations can add up over time.
- Consider the scale consciously – what seems insignificant in one context may be crucial in another.

title: Women Are Wonderful Effect – when women are seen more positively than men
description:
Do you think women are naturally kinder, more honest, and caring? That’s Women Are Wonderful Effect – the tendency to associate more positive attributes with women than with men, regardless of actual behavior.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Social stereotypes – society expects women to be more gentle and virtuous, even when behavior doesn’t match expectations.
- Judging actions – the same behavior is seen differently: a strict man is ‘harsh,’ while a strict woman is ‘fair.’
- Media & culture – female characters in films are often portrayed as morally superior to men.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Judge people by their actions, not their gender – moral qualities aren’t determined by sex.
- Watch for double standards – if men and women do the same thing but are perceived differently, bias is at play.
- Look at real data – a positive bias toward one group doesn’t always mean objectivity.

title: Authority Bias – when you trust authority figures, even if they’re wrong
description:
Do you tend to trust experts, bosses, or celebrities just because they hold authority? That’s Authority Bias – the tendency to overvalue the accuracy of influential figures’ opinions, regardless of their actual validity.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Medicine – people blindly follow doctors or ‘TV experts,’ even when their advice contradicts science.
- Work & management – employees make decisions based on a boss’s opinion rather than factual evidence.
- Politics & media – statements from public figures are accepted as truth without critical analysis.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Separate authority from facts – a high status doesn’t make someone automatically right.
- Ask questions – if something sounds off, check the source and logic behind it.
- Trust, but verify – even experts make mistakes, and authority is no substitute for critical thinking.

title: Halo Effect – when one good trait overshadows everything else
description:
Do you assume someone is smart just because they’re confident and charismatic? That’s Halo Effect – the tendency to attribute extra positive traits to a person based on one appealing characteristic.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Work & career – charismatic candidates seem more competent, even with less experience.
- Appearance – attractive people are perceived as kinder and smarter, regardless of actual traits.
- Media & society – celebrities known for one skill are often seen as experts in unrelated areas.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Focus on facts, not first impressions – one great trait doesn’t mean someone excels at everything.
- Separate skills from personality – confidence doesn’t always equal competence.
- Don’t judge by looks – attractiveness and charm can hide flaws.

title: Actor-Observer Bias – when you blame circumstances for yourself but personality for others
description:
Late to a meeting? Well, traffic was terrible! Someone else is late? They must be irresponsible. That’s Actor-Observer Bias – the tendency to blame our own behavior on external circumstances while attributing others’ actions to their personality.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Work & career – if a colleague fails a task, they’re lazy; if you fail, it’s because you didn’t have enough time.
- Driving – other drivers are reckless, but when you make a mistake, it was ‘necessary.’
- Relationships – if your partner is moody, it’s ‘just who they are’; if you’re moody, it’s because you had a tough day.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Apply the same standards to yourself and others – people face tough situations too.
- Consider the context – personality isn’t always the cause of behavior.
- Flip the situation – how would you explain your own behavior in the same case?

title: Defensive Attribution – when you blame more as the harm gets worse or feels personal
description:
Do you feel a stronger urge to blame someone when an accident is severe or hits close to home? That’s Defensive Attribution – the tendency to assign more blame to a harm-doer as the outcome worsens or if you relate to the victim.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Justice & punishment – people demand harsher punishment if they feel they could have been the victim.
- Car accidents – the worse the crash, the more the driver is seen as not just guilty but reckless.
- Moral judgments – when something bad happens to a loved one, there’s a strong urge to find someone to blame, even if it was an accident.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Judge actions, not just outcomes – a bigger tragedy doesn’t always mean bigger blame.
- Be aware of emotional influence – the closer you feel to the victim, the harder it is to stay objective.
- Separate intent from accident – not all bad things happen because someone meant them to.

title: Extrinsic Incentives Bias – when you think others work for rewards, but you work for passion
description:
Do you think your colleagues work just for money while you do it out of passion? That’s Extrinsic Incentives Bias – the tendency to believe others are motivated by external rewards while you act out of genuine interest.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Work & career – people assume their colleagues are driven by bonuses, while they themselves are dedicated to the job.
- Education – students believe others study for grades, but they do it for knowledge.
- Charity & altruism – someone else donates for publicity, but you do it because you genuinely care?

💡 How to avoid it?
- Don’t see yourself as special and others as transactional – everyone has both intrinsic and extrinsic motivations.
- Put yourself in their shoes – maybe your coworker also loves their job, not just the paycheck.
- Don’t devalue others’ efforts – just because someone benefits doesn’t mean their motives aren’t sincere.

title: Group Attribution Error – when you judge a whole group based on one person
description:
Did you meet one rude tourist and assume their entire country is like that? That’s Group Attribution Error – the tendency to believe that an individual’s behavior represents their entire group.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Nations & stereotypes – encountering one impolite foreigner leads to assumptions about their whole country.
- Politics & work – if one employee makes a mistake, people assume the whole company is incompetent.
- Group decisions – thinking a final decision reflects everyone’s opinion, even if most disagreed.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Don’t generalize from a single case – one person ≠ an entire group.
- Consider the context – individual actions depend on many factors, not just group identity.
- Check real data – if you want to understand a group, rely on research, not just anecdotes.

title: Hostile Attribution Bias – when you see hostility even where there is none
description:
Did someone bump into you, and you assume it was on purpose? That’s Hostile Attribution Bias – the tendency to see neutral or accidental actions as intentionally aggressive.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Communication & conflicts – an innocent joke seems like an attack, and a neutral tone feels cold and aggressive.
- Work & colleagues – if a coworker doesn’t greet you, they must be ignoring you (or maybe they were just lost in thought?).
- Driving & traffic – if someone cuts you off, it’s not a mistake, it’s a personal insult… or is it?

💡 How to avoid it?
- Consider innocent explanations first – most people aren’t plotting against you.
- Don’t jump to conclusions – emotions can make you see hostility where none exists.
- Ask instead of assuming – if someone’s behavior seems off, clarify before making judgments.

title: Intentionality Bias – when you assume everything is done on purpose
description:
Did someone step on your foot, and you assume they did it on purpose? That’s Intentionality Bias – the tendency to believe people’s actions are deliberate, even when they’re accidental.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Social situations – if a friend doesn’t reply, they must be ignoring you, rather than just being busy.
- Work & colleagues – if your boss forgot about your report, it’s not because they’re overwhelmed, but because they want to fire you.
- Driving & traffic – if someone brakes suddenly, it’s not bad luck, it’s a personal attack!

💡 How to avoid it?
- Separate accidents from intentions – not everything happens on purpose.
- Ask instead of assuming – if something seems off, clarify before jumping to conclusions.
- Remember, you’re not the center of the universe – most people aren’t going out of their way to mess with you.

title: Just-World Hypothesis – when you believe people get what they deserve
description:
Do you think poor people are just lazy and rich people earned their success? That’s Just-World Hypothesis – the tendency to believe everything happens fairly, even when events are random or unjust.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Social inequality – assuming that unsuccessful people deserve their fate while successful people earned everything fairly.
- Victim blaming – believing that if something bad happens to someone, they must have ‘brought it on themselves.’
- Work & career – thinking that promotions always go to the most deserving, rather than those who were just in the right place at the right time.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Accept that the world is chaotic – effort and morality don’t always determine outcomes.
- Question simple explanations – failure isn’t always the result of mistakes, and success isn’t always the result of talent.
- Consider systemic factors – circumstances, environment, and luck play a huge role in life outcomes.

title: Moral Luck – when you judge morality based on the outcome, not the intent
description:
If someone accidentally hits a pedestrian, they’re a terrible person, but if they just ran a red light and nothing happened – it’s ‘no big deal’? That’s Moral Luck – the tendency to judge actions based on their outcome rather than the intent behind them.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Law & punishment – a drunk driver who doesn’t hit anyone is seen as ‘lucky,’ while one who causes harm is judged far more harshly, even if they took the same risk.
- Work & business – two people make the same risky decision, but the one who succeeds is a ‘genius,’ while the one who fails is ‘reckless.’
- Politics & leadership – if a policy works, its creator is a hero; if it fails, they’re incompetent, even if their decisions were identical.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Look at intent, not just the result – sometimes people do everything right but still fail due to bad luck.
- Compare similar situations – if two people make the same choice but only one faces consequences, it doesn’t make them morally different.
- Recognize the role of randomness – circumstances have a huge impact, and outcomes aren’t always in a person’s control.

title: Puritanical Bias – when people blame morality instead of circumstances
description:
Do you believe poor people are just lazy? That’s Puritanical Bias – the tendency to blame negative outcomes on personal morality rather than external, societal, or economic factors.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Wealth & success – assuming rich people worked harder, while the poor are responsible for their own failures.
- Addiction & illness – seeing addiction as a lack of willpower instead of a complex mix of biology and environment.
- Crime & justice – judging criminals solely for their choices while ignoring the conditions they grew up in.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Consider systemic factors – success and failure are often shaped by external influences.
- Don’t reduce everything to morality – people make mistakes due to circumstances, not just weak character.
- Look at the full context – before judging, consider what external pressures might have played a role.

title: Self-Serving Bias – when success is yours, but failure is someone else’s fault
description:
Got promoted? That’s your talent! Didn’t get promoted? Must be your boss’s bias. That’s Self-Serving Bias – the tendency to credit yourself for successes but blame external factors for failures.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Work & career – if a project succeeds, you take the credit; if it fails, it’s the team’s fault.
- School & exams – good grade? You’re smart. Bad grade? The teacher was unfair.
- Sports & competition – if you win, it’s due to your preparation; if you lose, the referee was biased or the conditions were bad.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Take responsibility for failures – not all mistakes are caused by external factors.
- Be honest with yourself – successes and failures are usually a mix of personal effort and external circumstances.
- Analyze feedback – if you always find external excuses, ask yourself if it’s preventing growth.

title: Ultimate Attribution Error – when you judge an entire group based on a few individuals
description:
If one person from a group does something bad, does that mean they’re all like that? That’s Ultimate Attribution Error – the tendency to attribute an individual’s actions to their entire group, especially for negative behavior.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Nations & ethnic groups – if one tourist is rude, people assume everyone from that country is the same.
- Political views – if one politician lies, their entire party must be dishonest.
- Workplace & teams – if one employee makes a mistake, the whole company is seen as incompetent.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Judge individuals, not labels – a single person doesn’t represent an entire group.
- Separate actions from identity – being part of a group doesn’t automatically make someone good or bad.
- Don’t generalize from one bad experience – one negative example doesn’t define a whole category.

title: Availability Cascade – when repeating something enough makes it feel true
description:
The more you hear an idea, the more true it seems? That’s Availability Cascade – a process where information starts feeling like fact simply because it’s repeated often enough.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Fake news & myths – false claims about health, finance, or science become ‘common knowledge’ just because they’re repeated frequently.
- Politics & propaganda – the more a leader is called a ‘hero’ or a ‘villain,’ the more people believe it, even without real evidence.
- Moral panic – society suddenly fears a nonexistent threat because media and social networks keep amplifying it.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Repetition ≠ truth – verify facts, even if you’ve heard them a hundred times.
- Be skeptical of popular beliefs – just because something sounds logical and is widely discussed doesn’t mean it’s true.
- Look for original sources – many widely accepted claims have no real scientific or historical basis.

title: Bandwagon Effect – when you believe or do something just because everyone else does
description:
Did everyone suddenly start wearing weird sneakers – and now you want them too? That’s Bandwagon Effect – the tendency to follow the majority, even without good reasons.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Fashion & trends – people buy products or use services just because they’re popular, not because they actually need them.
- Investing & finance – hype around stocks or crypto leads people to invest without understanding real value.
- Politics & beliefs – supporting ideas or candidates simply because the majority does, not because of informed decisions.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Ask yourself: do I actually need this? – popularity doesn’t equal quality.
- Check the facts – the majority can be wrong, especially in complex topics.
- Make conscious choices – better to stand out than blindly follow the crowd.

title: Courtesy Bias – when you hide your real opinion to avoid offending others
description:
Told your friend their new haircut looks great, even though you hate it? That’s Courtesy Bias – the tendency to soften your opinion to avoid hurting others’ feelings.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Feedback & reviews – people praise bad service or low-quality products just to be polite.
- Work & career – employees hesitate to criticize a boss’s bad ideas out of fear of conflict.
- Personal relationships – agreeing with friends out of politeness, even when you actually disagree.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Be honest but tactful – you can express your opinion without being rude.
- Know when truth matters more than politeness – especially when quality or success is at stake.
- Don’t be afraid to disagree – respectful disagreement is better than empty compliments.

title: Groupthink – when harmony matters more than the right decision
description:
Did everyone in your team agree on a bad idea without questioning it? That’s Groupthink – the tendency to sacrifice critical thinking for group unity and harmony.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Business & management – projects fail because no one dares to challenge a bad idea.
- Politics & leadership – catastrophic decisions happen when leaders aren’t questioned.
- Social groups – people go along with the majority even when they know it’s wrong.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Encourage dissent – criticism helps prevent collective mistakes.
- Seek alternative opinions – if everyone thinks alike, it’s a warning sign.
- Look outside the group – an outsider’s perspective can reveal blind spots.

title: Groupshift – when groups make riskier or safer choices than individuals
description:
Did your team start off cautious but end up playing it ultra-safe? Or did they go from slightly risky to full-on reckless? That’s Groupshift – the tendency for group decisions to become more extreme than individual opinions.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Business & investing – a board discusses a bold strategy and ends up making an insanely risky move.
- Politics & activism – groups with conservative or radical views tend to become even more extreme over time.
- Team decision-making – collective choices sometimes swing between being overly cautious or dangerously aggressive.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Slow down decision-making – rushed discussions lead to extremes.
- Appoint a ‘devil’s advocate’ – someone should actively challenge the group’s reasoning.
- Break discussions into stages – gather individual opinions first, then compare with the group consensus.

title: Truth Bias – when you believe people, even when they might be lying
description:
Do you naturally trust what people say? That’s Truth Bias – the tendency to assume information is honest, even without evidence.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Lies & manipulation – people are less likely to doubt words from familiar or authoritative figures, even when misleading.
- Financial scams – investors trust ‘promising projects’ because no one thinks they’ll be deceived.
- Personal life – believing promises, even when they’ve been broken multiple times.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Trust, but verify – facts matter more than words, especially in important matters.
- Focus on logic, not emotions – people tend to believe comforting stories, even if they don’t hold up.
- Remember that everyone can be wrong – honesty ≠ truth, even if someone believes what they say.

title: Ingroup Bias – when what’s ‘ours’ is always better than what’s ‘theirs’
description:
Do you think your team’s way is the best and anything external isn’t worth considering? That’s Ingroup Bias, also known as ‘Not Invented Here’ – the tendency to reject ideas, research, and products simply because they come from outside your group.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Business & technology – companies refuse to adopt external solutions, even if they’re more efficient.
- Science & research – scholars dismiss data from ‘outside their school’ regardless of its validity.
- Politics & society – people reject policies or innovations from other cultures simply because ‘that’s not how we do it.’

💡 How to avoid it?
- Evaluate quality, not origin – a good idea remains good no matter who came up with it.
- Stay open to alternatives – external methods and insights can be valuable.
- Watch your reasoning – if your only argument is ‘it’s not ours,’ you might be letting bias cloud your judgment.

title: Outgroup Homogeneity Bias – when ‘they’re all the same,’ but ‘we’re all unique’
description:
Do you feel like your group is diverse, but other groups are all the same? That’s Outgroup Homogeneity Bias – the tendency to see members of your own group as individuals, while viewing outsiders as uniform.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- National stereotypes – ‘All French people love wine’ or ‘All Germans are punctual,’ when in reality, individuals vary.
- Politics – supporters of the other party seem ‘all equally misguided,’ while your side consists of ‘independent thinkers.’
- Work & competition – your company has diverse talents, but competitors all seem identical.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Replace generalizations with facts – before saying ‘they’re all like that,’ ask yourself if you have real evidence.
- Put yourself in their shoes – would you like being stereotyped the same way?
- Engage with different people – personal experience is the best way to break stereotypes.

title: Assumed Similarity Bias – when you think others are more like you than they really are
description:
Do you assume most people think like you? That’s Assumed Similarity Bias – the tendency to believe others share your perspectives, preferences, and values more than they actually do.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Work & negotiations – you assume colleagues or clients agree with your ideas, but their priorities might be completely different.
- Friendships & relationships – you’re shocked when a friend or partner makes a choice you would never make.
- Politics & social beliefs – it feels like ‘all reasonable people’ think like you, even though the real range of opinions is much broader.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Ask instead of assuming – just because you share some interests doesn’t mean they think like you.
- Be open to different viewpoints – expecting similarity makes it harder to understand others.
- Check your expectations – if you’re surprised by someone’s choice, you might have assumed they were ‘just like you.’

title: Outgroup Favoritism – when other groups seem better than your own
description:
Do you feel like other groups always have it better – their culture, their people, their values? That’s Outgroup Favoritism – the tendency for socially disadvantaged groups to favor and even prefer other communities over their own.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Cultural stereotypes – believing that ‘over there’ everything is higher quality, more honest, or more progressive than ‘here.’
- Self-esteem & identity – undervaluing one’s own group while admiring external norms and traditions.
- Politics & society – supporting privileged groups, even when it works against one’s own interests.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Compare objectively – every group has strengths and weaknesses, not just an idealized image.
- Recognize the power of stereotypes – society may push certain groups as ‘better,’ but that doesn’t make it true.
- Judge people individually – group membership alone doesn’t make someone better or worse.

title: Pygmalion Effect – when others’ expectations shape your success (or failure)
description:
Do you perform better when people believe in you? That’s Pygmalion Effect – a psychological phenomenon where others’ expectations (positive or negative) influence your actual performance and behavior.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Education – if a teacher believes a student is talented, they perform better, even if all students start at the same level.
- Work & career – employees trusted with challenging tasks tend to grow professionally faster.
- Personal life – if people see you as strong and capable, over time, you start acting accordingly.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Evaluate yourself objectively – don’t let low expectations from others hold you back.
- Surround yourself with believers – having people who trust in you can actually boost your achievements.
- Use it intentionally – if you lead or mentor others, your expectations can shape their success.

title: Reactance – when being told ‘no’ makes you want to do it even more
description:
Does being told ‘no’ make you want to do it even more? That’s Reactance – a psychological response where attempts to limit your freedom trigger resistance and a desire to do the opposite.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Advertising & marketing – phrases like ‘limited edition’ or ‘only for VIPs’ make you want the product more.
- Rules & laws – the stricter the restriction, the stronger the temptation to break it, even if you weren’t interested before.
- Personal relationships – when someone tells you not to talk to someone or do something, you suddenly want to do it even more.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Pause before reacting – if you feel resistance, ask yourself: ‘Do I really want this, or am I just reacting to the restriction?’
- Replace rebellion with conscious choice – sometimes rules exist for a reason, even if they feel restrictive.
- Use the effect strategically – if you want someone to do something, try ‘forbidding’ them from doing it.

title: Reactive Devaluation – when an idea seems bad just because of who suggested it
description:
Do you reject a good idea just because it came from your opponent? That’s Reactive Devaluation – the tendency to dismiss proposals just because they come from an ‘undesirable’ source, even if they’re beneficial.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Politics & negotiations – people reject compromises simply because they come from the other side.
- Workplace conflicts – companies ignore good suggestions from competitors, even when they could be valuable.
- Personal relationships – if a rival or disliked person makes a suggestion, it feels suspicious by default.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Focus on the idea, not the person – even someone you dislike can offer valuable insights.
- Imagine the idea came from an ally – would your judgment change?
- Separate emotions from logic – don’t reject beneficial solutions just because of personal bias.

title: Social Comparison Bias – when you favor people who aren’t a threat to your own strengths
description:
Do you hire people who won’t challenge you rather than those who are truly the best? That’s Social Comparison Bias – the tendency to favor candidates who don’t threaten your skills or status.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Hiring decisions – managers avoid hiring talented people out of fear of being overshadowed.
- Team building – choosing ‘safe’ colleagues instead of those who could actually improve results.
- Leadership & promotions – leaders hesitate to promote those who might become future rivals.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Prioritize value over safety – working with strong people leads to better outcomes.
- Don’t fear competition – smart, talented colleagues help you grow, not hinder you.
- Replace fear with strategy – surround yourself with those who strengthen the team, not just those who feel ‘comfortable.’

title: Shared Information Bias – when groups focus on what they all know, ignoring new insights
description:
Does your team spend hours discussing obvious facts while ignoring a crucial detail known only to a few? That’s Shared Information Bias – the tendency for groups to focus on what everyone already knows instead of sharing unique insights.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Meetings & planning – teams discuss well-known issues while overlooking fresh perspectives.
- Strategic decision-making – instead of analyzing new data, groups waste time reiterating the obvious.
- Science & medicine – clinicians and researchers rely on established knowledge, sometimes missing groundbreaking discoveries.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Actively seek new voices – ask questions to uncover missing insights.
- Create space for unique ideas – encourage people to share what others may not know.
- Focus on what hasn’t been discussed – challenge the group with: ‘What are we overlooking?’

title: Worse-Than-Average Effect – when you assume you're worse than others at difficult tasks
description:
Do you assume everyone else is better than you at difficult tasks? That’s Worse-Than-Average Effect – the tendency to underestimate your own competence in challenging activities, even when you have the skills.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Studying & exams – you're sure you’ll fail the test, even though you studied as much as others.
- New skills – afraid to try programming, languages, or driving because ‘that’s for smarter people.’
- Work & career – you assume colleagues will figure things out faster, even when you start at the same level.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Compare yourself to facts, not fears – you’re likely better than you think.
- Remember, hard things are hard for everyone – others may just hide their doubts better.
- Just start and see – experience will prove you’re more capable than you expect.

title: Cryptomnesia – when you think you came up with something new, but it’s actually an old memory
description:
Did you come up with a brilliant idea, only to realize you’d heard it before? That’s Cryptomnesia – when a forgotten memory resurfaces as an original thought because you don’t recognize it as a memory.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Creativity & innovation – you believe you wrote an original song or article, but it closely resembles something you heard before.
- Work & brainstorming – you propose a ‘new’ solution, only for colleagues to remind you it was suggested before.
- Conversations & debates – you unknowingly repeat someone else’s argument, convinced it was your own thought.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Fact-check yourself – before claiming an idea as yours, try to recall if you’ve encountered it before.
- Track your sources of inspiration – this helps keep record of where your ideas originate.
- Be open to correction – if someone points out your idea isn’t new, take it as an opportunity to learn rather than a setback.

title: False Memory – when you ‘remember’ something that never happened
description:
Are you sure you’ve been to a place as a child, but your parents insist you never were? That’s False Memory – when imagination, stories from others, or time create memories of events that never actually happened.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Childhood memories – vivid childhood scenes may be brain-constructed based on stories rather than real experiences.
- Eyewitness testimony – people genuinely believe they saw something that never happened, especially under leading questions or suggestion.
- Personal stories – over time, details shift, and you may recall events differently than they actually occurred.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Be cautious with confidence – just because a memory feels real doesn’t mean it is.
- Verify facts – if an event is important, check for proof (photos, diaries, eyewitness accounts).
- Understand how memory works – the brain constantly edits memories, filling in gaps with assumptions.

title: Social Cryptomnesia – when you remember change but forget who fought for it
description:
Do you enjoy rights and freedoms but can’t recall who fought for them? That’s Social Cryptomnesia – when society recognizes that change has happened but forgets how it occurred and who made it possible.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Civil rights – people take freedoms and equality for granted, forgetting those who fought for them.
- Feminism & women’s rights – many assume women ‘always’ had the right to work and vote, ignoring the struggle behind it.
- Technological breakthroughs – people use the internet and smartphones without knowing who made them possible.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Learn the history of change – major shifts don’t happen on their own.
- Acknowledge the pioneers – remember who actually fought for what we now take for granted.
- Spread awareness – remind others that behind every right and convenience, there were sacrifices.

title: Source Confusion – when you remember information but forget where it came from
description:
Do you remember a fact but can’t recall whether you read it in a research paper or a social media comment? That’s Source Confusion – the tendency to misremember where information came from, distorting our memories.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Fake news & rumors – you might accept a rumor as fact if you forget it came from an unreliable source.
- False memories – you may believe you witnessed an event firsthand when you actually learned about it from the news.
- Work & learning – hard to recall whether you came up with an idea yourself or heard it from a colleague.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Verify the source – if the information matters, make sure it’s credible.
- Track your knowledge sources – write down where you read or heard key information.
- Be cautious with memories – just because you remember something doesn’t mean it happened exactly that way.

title: Suggestibility – when you ‘remember’ things just because someone suggested them
description:
Did someone ask, ‘Do you remember getting lost in a store as a child?’ and now you’re convinced it happened? That’s Suggestibility – the tendency to mistake others’ suggestions for real memories.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Criminal investigations – witnesses ‘remember’ details of a crime that never happened due to leading questions.
- Childhood memories – a child is told they loved a certain toy, and over time, they truly believe it.
- Medicine & therapy – under hypnosis or improper therapy, patients may ‘recall’ events that never actually occurred.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Be skeptical of ‘recovered’ details – especially if someone suggested them first.
- Separate facts from suggestion – if you don’t clearly remember something, consider that it may have been ‘planted.’
- Analyze how the memory formed – is it truly your own experience or a reaction to someone’s words?

title: The Perky Effect – when reality blends with imagination
description:
Did you vividly imagine skydiving and later wonder if it actually happened? That’s The Perky Effect – when real images or experiences influence imagined ones, making it hard to distinguish fantasy from reality.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Dreams vs. memories – you’re convinced you talked to someone, but it was just a dream.
- Visualization vs. reality – you imagined doing something so clearly that you believe you actually did it.
- Media & false memories – something seen in a movie or commercial is later misremembered as a personal experience.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Filter your memories – if a detail feels too vivid but the source is unclear, it might be imagined.
- Reality-check yourself – if in doubt, ask: ‘Did this really happen?’
- Be mindful of visualization – the more vividly you picture an event, the easier it is to mistake it for reality.

title: Availability Bias – when recent or vivid examples seem more important
description:
Did you hear about a plane crash and now fear flying, even though car accidents are far more common? That’s Availability Bias – the tendency to give greater importance to examples that are easy to recall, rather than those that are statistically relevant.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- News & fears – dramatic events (disasters, crimes) create the illusion that they happen more often than they actually do.
- Financial decisions – if someone recently got rich from crypto, it seems like an easy way to make money.
- Health & medicine – a celebrity’s illness is perceived as more common than it really is.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Look at statistics, not headlines – vivid stories don’t always reflect reality.
- Check the proportions – frequent events are less memorable but often more relevant.
- Remember: rarity makes things noticeable – just because something is widely discussed doesn’t mean it happens often.

title: Bizarreness Effect – when weird things stick in memory better than ordinary ones
description:
Do you remember a person in a banana costume better than one in a regular suit? That’s Bizarreness Effect – the tendency to recall unusual information more easily than common information.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Learning & memory – strange or absurd associations help retain information more effectively.
- News & media – shocking headlines stick in memory, even when the information isn’t important.
- False memories – due to the bizarreness effect, fake but vivid events may feel real.

💡 How to use it?
- Create bizarre associations – the weirder, the better for memorization.
- Filter what you remember – just because it sticks doesn’t mean it’s important.
- Be cautious with memories – strange details may feel more real than they actually are.

title: Boundary Extension – when your memory ‘zooms out’ beyond what you actually saw
description:
Do you look at a photo and later recall seeing more details than were actually there? That’s Boundary Extension – the tendency to remember the background of an image as more expansive than it really was.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Perceiving photographs – you recall a full landscape in a photo, even though only a small section was framed.
- Eyewitness testimony – people insist they saw the whole scene, even if their field of view was limited.
- Past memories – your brain ‘fills in the gaps,’ making you believe you saw more than you actually did.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Trust facts, not feelings – your memory isn’t always accurate.
- Double-check images – compare what you remember with the actual photo.
- Remember that your brain auto-fills details – the more familiar a scene, the stronger the effect.

title: Childhood Amnesia – why we forget our earliest years
description:
Can you remember your third birthday? Probably not. That’s Childhood Amnesia – the natural inability to retain memories from the first few years of life.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- False memories – many ‘memories’ of infancy are actually based on stories from parents or photos.
- Emotional events – even significant moments (like moving to a new home) fade if they happened before age 4.
- Brain development – the neural connections needed for long-term memory aren’t fully formed in early childhood.

💡 How to understand it?
- The brain doesn’t store early memories like adult ones – and that’s completely normal.
- Early experiences shape us, even if we don’t recall them – emotions and interactions still influence personality.
- Photos and stories help ‘rebuild’ the past – but be mindful, not all memories are real.

title: Confirmation Bias – when you only notice what supports your beliefs
description:
Do you read news that only confirms what you already believe? That’s Confirmation Bias – the tendency to seek, remember, and interpret information in ways that align with existing beliefs.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Politics & media – people choose sources that reinforce their views while ignoring alternative perspectives.
- Investing & business – investors focus only on data that confirms their decisions, missing warning signs.
- Personal life – if you think someone is unreliable, you’ll notice only their mistakes, ignoring their good actions.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Read opposing viewpoints – challenge yourself by considering different arguments.
- Question your own beliefs – ask yourself: ‘What if I’m wrong?’
- Follow facts, not emotions – truth isn’t defined by how comfortable it makes you feel.

title: Conservatism Bias – when your memory downplays extremes
description:
Do you remember heavy rain, but in reality, it was a full-blown storm? That’s Conservatism Bias – the tendency to recall high values (like probability or frequency) as lower than they were and low values as higher.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Historical events – disasters or crises seem less severe than they felt at the time.
- Finance & risk – investors underestimate past market crashes but overestimate minor fluctuations.
- Personal success & failure – achievements feel less impressive, and failures seem less dramatic over time.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Trust data, not memory – your brain naturally smooths out extremes.
- Record key events – writing down numbers and details helps evaluate them objectively later.
- Remember that time dulls emotions – past stress or joy often feels weaker in hindsight.

title: Consistency Bias – when you believe you’ve always thought the way you do now
description:
Are you convinced you’ve always supported healthy living, but ten years ago you ate fast food daily? That’s Consistency Bias – the tendency to remember past beliefs and behaviors as being consistent with your current ones.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- Politics & beliefs – people think their opinions never changed, even when past evidence suggests otherwise.
- Habits & behavior – you feel like you’ve always been disciplined, but your younger self would disagree.
- Relationships & work – you recall always valuing your job or partner, though you had doubts in the past.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Review old records – journals, posts, or conversations may reveal how your views evolved.
- Accept mental growth – it’s okay to change opinions rather than pretending you’ve always been the same.
- Be honest with yourself – ask, ‘What did I actually think back then?’

title: Continued Influence Effect – when misinformation sticks, even after being debunked
description:
